speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will just pause for a few minutes.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I take full responsibility for this mistake and I deeply regret the consternation, the anxiety that was caused by my mistake.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In Parliament last month, the Minister for Home Affairs and I stated that the use of TraceTogether data in investigations or criminal proceedings would be restricted to serious offences.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This Bill before us gives legal force to these statements.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, I do not know exactly when the pandemic will end.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: What I do know is that contact tracing, augmented by digital tools, enables us to quickly break the chains of transmission by identifying and isolating close contacts.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is precisely why we need high participation rates in digital contact tracing.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Contact tracing is traditionally a manual, painstaking and very resource-intensive task.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Members of the House may recall that – cast your minds back a year ago – at the start of the pandemic, when the number of cases started to grow.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we had to rapidly expand the pool of contact tracers to keep up with the load.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We even had to call in reinforcements from the Singapore Armed Forces.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But we all knew that this would not be sustainable if the numbers continued to rise.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, we realised, very early on, that we needed to make better use of both technology and data, including especially proximity data, generated from Bluetooth technology, in order to help our contact tracers carry out their work more effectively and efficiently.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And I say this with the experience of SARS 17 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: SARS had much fewer cases than COVID-19 and it was a manual contact tracing system.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We would not have been able to cope with the sheer volume this time if we were still using the methods of 17 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This was why we conceptualised and introduced TraceTogether – to reduce the time and the resources needed to collect some of these essential data for contact tracing.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And, if I may add, these efforts have paid off.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This means that people who have been exposed, or potentially exposed, are isolated more swiftly.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It reduces the probability of them passing on the virus to their family members, friends and the community at large.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And where there is widespread adoption of digital contact tracing, the enhanced effectiveness can be very significant.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In the recent Royal Caribbean Quantum of the Seas case, the use of TraceTogether data helped MOH to quickly identify more than three-quarters of the close contacts – although thankfully, in this case, it turned out to be a false positive.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: TraceTogether has also enabled us to trace contacts more comprehensively and to identify many contacts whom the person may not have recalled meeting or even realised that he had been in close contact with.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And this is particularly so, when you are with someone whom you do not already know.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The probability of your forgetting that interaction is much higher.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: TraceTogether was always designed for contact tracing purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And this is obvious, if you consider the safeguards and the features of the system.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: TraceTogether only collects proximity data, which is necessary in order to identify close contacts.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It does not collect GPS data; it does not collect movement data.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The token does not even have cellular connectivity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These were conscious design decisions made at conception.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Furthermore, the app and the token only keep a temporary record, in an encrypted form, locally on the device itself.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And this data is automatically purged after 25 days.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Government also intends to deactivate TraceTogether, along with the other digital contact tracing programmes, once the pandemic is over.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The GovTech engineers and I took great pains to create an app that was fundamentally privacy protecting at its core – privacy by design.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We invited experts to come and tear down the TraceTogether token to prove this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Perhaps, I was so enamoured by what I thought was the ingenuity and brilliance of this that I got blindsided.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Prof Ang Peng Hwa of NTU very elegantly described our ethical dilemma as one in which we are dealing with a choice between "right" versus "right".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: A choice between "right" and "wrong" is very easy to make.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But in this case, it is right to protect public health by protecting the data in TraceTogether.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But it is also right, and just as important, to protect public safety, especially when it comes to serious crimes – "right" versus "right".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It would indeed be unconscionable to inhibit the ability of the Police to act, when it comes to a serious offence that affects someone's life or safety.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Someone came up to me and said, "Think about the example of a kidnapped child.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And all that was left was a dropped phone or a token.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And if that mother brought that token or phone to the Police, would it be right for us to say, 'No, we cannot and would not do anything about it.'?" In fact, it would be untenable – to adopt a purist ideological stance and to deliberately refuse to check that data and pursue all leads available.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore is one of the safest countries in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our people walk the streets safely, day or night, alone or in groups, with peace of mind, precisely because there is high trust in an effective Police Force that always acts for the public good, that legally pursues all information and leads available to solve and to prevent crimes.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We cannot take this safety and security that we value so much for granted even in the midst of this pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This Bill sets out what Minister Shanmugam and I said in Parliament last month.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singaporeans also understand and support the Police's continued access to such data for investigations or criminal proceedings in respect of serious offences, to bring perpetrators of crime to justice and to protect public safety and security.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are moving this Bill on a Certificate of Urgency, so that it may come into effect as soon as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Clause 7 of the Bill introduces section 80 to define "personal contact tracing data" to mean "entry or exit records, proximity information or other data collected using any digital contact tracing tool or combination of digital contact tracing tools, that is part of a digital contact tracing system, and which, by itself or with other information, identifies any individual".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Basically, it means, the key point is, data that is personally identifiable.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The "digital contact tracing systems" covered by the Bill are listed in the Sixth Schedule.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This will include TraceTogether, SafeEntry and BluePass insofar as it is interoperable with TraceTogether.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: SafeEntry, as Members are aware, is a digital equivalent of the visitor record logs.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: BluePass is a contact tracing system, developed by the private sector, that is capable of interoperating with TraceTogether in order to support the national programme.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are concerned with protecting personal contact tracing data in the Government’s national digital contact tracing systems, and we will treat all data in the same way, however it enters the national system.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Section 84 specifies that the Minister may add to the list of "digital contact tracing systems" if new systems or additional systems are created.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: However, any removal from the Sixth Schedule will require Parliamentary approval.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This means that the Government cannot unilaterally remove any digital contact tracing system from the restrictions imposed by this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Clause 7 of the Bill introduces subsection 82(1), which specifies that the data may only be used to "carry out or facilitate contact tracing".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These are offences of a significant severity and/or pose an immediate threat to life or public safety, such as the use of firearms, dangerous weapons, terrorism, murder, drug offences that attract the death penalty, kidnapping and rape.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Government cannot amend this list of offences in the Seventh Schedule without coming back to Parliament for approval.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Third, the Government may not use the data for any purpose other than those mentioned, regardless of any other written law requiring or allowing the disclosure of the data.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Just in case "I don't know what I don't know." This is added assurance.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This will give added reassurance that there are no further scenarios where public agencies may use the data apart from the purposes stated explicitly in this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Clause 7 of the Bill introduces subsection 82(8) which provides for the Minister to specify a date after which a digital contact tracing system is no longer required to prevent or control the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The data administrator must then delete any personal contact tracing data which is no longer required.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have also built other safeguards into our digital contact tracing systems.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This 25-day timeline is set based on the advice of our medical professionals, to account for the incubation period of the virus, which we currently estimate to be 14 days, and the time taken from the onset of symptoms and for the patient to visit a doctor and get tested and, if positive, to notify MOH.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This data retention period could change on the advice of medical experts, if the virus continues to evolve and we have a better understanding of the disease, the virus and its incubation period.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But the point here is that we will stand guided on the basis of science and medicine.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Before I conclude my speech, I need to remind you that there are two other sections related to the Ministry of Health and Ministry of Law.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Part 7 provides the legal basis for the Minister for Health to make regulations to prevent or control the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These regulations underpin the safe management measures adopted since the circuit breaker last year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As this pandemic will not go away soon, it is imperative that we remain vigilant and continue with safe management measures in our daily lives.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The SLA is working to operationalise the Rental Relief Framework.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is crucial because the virus is a clear, present and, in fact, on a global scale, a growing threat.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And it will remain so for some time.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, we cannot afford to be distracted from our fight against COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We need to rally together, look out for one another, protect public health and safety even as we try carefully to re-open our economy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, I will talk about the Government's error in not realising that section 20 of the Criminal Procedure Code applies to TraceTogether data.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, I will speak on the carving out of the seven categories of offences in the Bill that permits the use of TraceTogether data and I will thereafter set out the Workers' Party's position on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Third, I will look to the longer term and reflect on the balance between the privacy rights of citizens and the growing power of the state and private companies in collecting and using data and personal information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe there is scope to learn important lessons from the fall-out that has ensued from the Government's admission that TraceTogether data could be used for investigatory purposes, a departure from earlier assurances that TraceTogether would only be used for contact tracing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A few Singaporeans have told me that if the Government had stated upfront that TraceTogether data would be used for the seven categories of serious crimes only, they would have been prepared to prioritise the use of TraceTogether because of the imperative of fighting an epidemic, even those who could have had residual privacy concerns could have been assuaged had the Government detailed the processes and accountability regime for using TraceTogether information in investigations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Why was there disquiet, unhappiness and even cynicism in some quarters at the Government's belated acknowledgement that TraceTogether can be used for criminal investigations as originally explained by Minister of State Desmond Tan in Parliament last month?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It comes down to a question of trust, the perceived lack of empathy over the public's privacy concerns and discomfort with sharing mobile phone data with the authorities without sufficient assurances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, from a very early stage the Government clearly contemplated that there would be privacy concerns with the use of TraceTogether for contact tracing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In his broadcast of 21 April 2020, the Prime Minister said that Singapore intended to make full use of IT, including TraceTogether, which would require everyone's cooperation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He added and, I quote, "There will be some privacy concerns, but we will have to weigh these against the benefits of being able to exit from the circuit breaker and stay open safely." In the months that followed, the public were told that the number of sign-ups to TraceTogether was not satisfactory.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As late as November, the multi-Ministerial Taskforce linked transiting to phase 3 in our fight against COVID-19 with requiring at least 70% of the population signing up for TraceTogether.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They further contend that if not Ministers, at least the officials in the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Ministry of Health and GovTech who conceived of TraceTogether would have known of the privacy considerations surrounding TraceTogether.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some go a step further in suspecting the Government of willful blindness on function creep, or worse, that the information surrounding the use of TraceTogether for criminal investigations may have been suppressed until the threshold of 70% of the population had downloaded the app or collected the TraceTogether token.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A separate group of Singaporeans queried whether there will be consequences for those who made this mistake in promising wrongly that TraceTogether would be used only for contact tracing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They believe the Government did not do its homework.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While there was no dishonesty or malice, there was a lack of care or diligence in accurately communicating the potential use of data collected by TraceTogether.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am sure Members have come across a range of opinions from residents in the course of their house visits or interactions with family and friends over the last few weeks on this matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I would like to ask two questions of the Government and, specifically, the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These questions are important for the House to understand at what point the Government determined that its original representations on the use of TraceTogether were misleading and whether it could have corrected the position and updated the public on its own initiative.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party's starting point on this matter is that Singapore is as close to a wartime scenario as most Singaporeans have seen in our lifetimes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This pandemic has exceeded in the living memory of older Singaporeans only by the far greater oppression of World War II.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In terms of its effects on the national consciousness, COVID-19 is perhaps on par with other upheavals such as the 1964 riots and Singapore's ejection from Malaysia in 1965.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Its scale and complexity have surpassed the SARS crisis of 2003.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In such a wartime scenario, the core question for this House is whether the change in the Government's position on TraceTogether data to allow for its use for serious crimes could compromise the fight against COVID-19 and jeopardise contact tracing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will make two points in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, while we know that TraceTogether data is critical for contact tracing, we need to ask whether TraceTogether data is vital for solving these seven categories of crimes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As it stands, the Police have an abundance of investigative tools.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They can forensically examine mobile phones and laptops that contain massive amounts of data other than TraceTogether.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They also have old-fashioned police work such as finding and interviewing witnesses using confidential informants, scrutinising the crime scene and collecting physical evidence for forensic analysis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is a legitimate view that these tools should be more than sufficient in detecting crime and securing convictions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is little or no doubt that TraceTogether would make things convenient for the Police.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But it is my view that convenience for the Police may not be a good enough reason to compromise the trust necessary to win the COVID-19 fight.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is an equally legitimate view that with the existing tools at their disposal, the Police are likely to have little, if any additional benefit from using TraceTogether data.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to hearing the Minister's answers to my questions so that we can know for sure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The answers will allow members of the public to appreciate the balance that is being struck between privacy and policing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On to my second point: would allowing these exceptions compromise the use of TraceTogether in fighting the pandemic?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Against the possible benefits of using TraceTogether for fighting crime, we need to compare the likely cost to our fight against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There was a public outcry after Minister of State Desmond Tan's reply on 4 January 2020 when Singaporeans found out that section 20 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) applied to TraceTogether and that the Government had backtracked on earlier assurances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some Singaporeans seemed placated when the Government announced a day later that the use of TraceTogether data would be restricted to the seven categories of crime.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, this House's knowledge of both support as well as resistance of Singaporeans is only anecdotal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, these numbers too can give a false sense of security insofar as our contact tracing efforts are concerned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, more than a few people have anecdotally shared online that they will use the TraceTogether app to gain entry to a place, only to turn off Bluetooth immediately after entering.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This clearly shows that a high level of downloads of the TraceTogether app does not necessarily translate to a high degree of continuous usage.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Those who choose to switch off their Bluetooth function could do so for various reasons, a common one being that people do not want to drain their phone battery and not necessarily because of privacy concerns.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We do not know for sure either way, but if the IPS report is indicative, privacy is more than likely to matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is therefore open to question whether the efficacy of TraceTogether for contact tracing could be compromised because of the Government's belated explanation on the use of TraceTogether data for investigative purposes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, I would like to inquire if the Government is able to track the number of users of the TraceTogether app who turn off their Bluetooth function after downloading the app and, separately, who turn it off after gaining entry to a building or premise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The answer to this question will determine whether TraceTogether is working as intended or whether the Government needs to comprehensively review the public buy-in and effectiveness of the TraceTogether app and token.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I now move on to the Workers' Party's position on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party is of the view that Singapore's number one priority should be to tackle the pandemic's public health and economic effects.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Anything that compromises this priority has to give way, unless there are overwhelming good reasons.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Other jurisdictions have taken a cleaner approach on contact tracing apps in line with the Government's original public statements that TraceTogether would be limited to contact tracing, period.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Personally and subject to the Minister's response on the centrality of TraceTogether data for policing, I, personally, would prefer aligning the use of TraceTogether with the Government's original emphatic assurances that TraceTogether would be used for contact tracing only.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is because of some Singaporeans' residual concerns over privacy and the established discomfort about sharing cellphone data.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am of the view that such an approach would also engender greater confidence given that a public conversation on privacy has hitherto not been ventilated in a significant way in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will return to that subject very shortly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The main reason is because the exceptions constitute a significant reduction of the wide ambit of section 20 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In other words, a Singaporean's right to privacy is better protected with this Bill than without it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim will speak further on the seven exceptions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The discomfort and distrust in some quarters generated by the belated disclosure on the applicability of section 20 of the Criminal Procedure Code to TraceTogether is somewhat or to some extent unsurprising.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would contend that across the population, there is a general lack of awareness about not just the Government's powers of data collection, investigation and privacy, but the rapid advance of predictive technologies for public use.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a society, many are relatively uninformed about legal or constitutional rights and responsibilities, to say nothing about the right to privacy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If we are already talking about a societal COVID-19 reset when this crisis passes, the Government should also review the lessons learnt from the roll-out of TraceTogether and, specifically, whether Singapore should actively appraise the balance between policing and citizen privacy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The mobile phone application WhatsApp recently found out the hard way what happens when people suddenly become suspicious about technology and privacy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When the company published new terms of service with a short deadline for acceptance, there was a huge backlash against WhatsApp and its corporate owner, Facebook.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: WhatsApp's experience shows that Singapore's experience with the TraceTogether issue is not unique.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Confidence in technological tools and the institutions that control them can be lost overnight.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This loss of trust engenders cynicism and push back from the public, and in an age where information travels instantaneously and fake news spreads at light speed, cynicism has to be taken very seriously and addressed squarely from a governance standpoint.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the first major debate of this parliamentary term, the Prime Minister addressed the House on Disease X, a possible outbreak even deadlier than COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The programme is meant to accelerate the production of diagnostic tools, therapies and vaccines once a major disease strikes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, medical preparedness is only part of the fight.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The other part is the battle for the trust and cooperation of the people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If Disease X strikes and another TraceTogether-type situation occurs, our fight against Disease X may be rendered ineffective and tragically thwarted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I call on the Government to initiate an immediate conversation on the balance between the state's collection and use of data against the individual's right of privacy because many of the new technologies with public repercussions have already been rolled out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: According to the latest Government Financial Statements, or GFS, MHA has invested in PolCam 3.0 and 4.0 whereas only PolCam 1.0 and 2.0 have entered the mainstream media lexicon.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Intrusive technology has already extended to other areas of governance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Let that sink in for a moment – behavioural analytics technology at a children's home.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What impact could befall a child if such data is hacked in a cybersecurity breach many years later?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How is the problem of bias, both from a technology perspective and a human interface angle, dealt with?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Who checks whether such information is secure or securely wiped?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And who has a right to review this information and for how long?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To counter skepticism and its resultant behaviours and to replace it with trust and cooperation, Singaporeans also need to better understand the necessity and ambit of data collection.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is especially so for a new generation who are more likely to be concerned about privacy and individual rights.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The public must also be assured that the data collected and used for investigative purposes have safeguards that are robust enough with independent and external checks and balances, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And it would be critical for the public to understand that in Singapore at least, regulation is marching in step with the evolution of newer and more intrusive policing and data collection technologies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is currently not the case in many parts of the world and there is an opportunity for Singapore to be a leader in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I would advance that there are important actions that the Government can undertake to better dispel doubts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, the Government should be forthcoming, without prompting, in informing the public about what data it collects and how it ensures the robustness and integrity of its processes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, the Government should ensure that our laws reassure Singaporean citizens and residents that investigatory powers and data collection are used for legitimate purposes and are subject to rigorous checks that protect us from the abuse of our personal data.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Moving forward, a review of our existing laws may be required to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first thing the Government could do to counter cynicism and create trust is to be forthcoming about what data it collects and the safeguards to prevent misuse of information in its possession.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government regularly asks information of tech giants like Facebook.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would reassure the public, in my view, if the Government could tell us what it has asked the tech companies for and for what purposes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This could be done on a regular basis through the Police's annual report, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the Government is forthcoming with such information, it will engender confidence that the Government has nothing to hide, is performing its role as a state should, and that its requests are for legitimate purposes in the interest of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans will also better appreciate the nature of the behind-the-scenes work that is done to keep Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I will make this point again: this awareness and confidence will aid us in our fight against future threats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second thing the Government could do is to conduct a broad review of the state's powers to collect data for the purposes of investigations in light of new technologies and consider how privacy concerns could be better balanced or accommodated within the legislation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Statutes like the Broadcasting Act and the Telecommunications Act and others give the Police powers akin to those in the Criminal Procedure Code, although specifically scoped for those Acts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even so, like the Criminal Procedure Code, the investigative powers of the relevant authorities are drafted broadly and do not include separate laws on how the exercise of these investigatory powers come with safeguards.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such safeguards would reassure the public that the state is acting legitimately and with sufficient regard for the individual's right to privacy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To build confidence between the citizen and the state in an era where the call for privacy will only get louder, other verification mechanisms can be considered.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would offer three suggestions in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One possibility for checking against abuse and engendering confidence can be the appointment of a neutral commissioner or an ombudsman to monitor the use of such powers by the Government and, in particular, law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another possibility is an omnibus legislation like the UK's Investigatory Powers Act.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This piece of legislation covers the acquisition and retention of data, including bulk personal datasets, and provides for how such material is dealt with, including oversight arrangements, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, the Government could include a key performance indicator in the Budget Book for each relevant Ministry that measures the public's confidence in the collection and use of data collected on the one hand, and the public's right to privacy on the other.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, it is important for me to restate that privacy concerns are not the domain of a small segment of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The international conversation has moved significantly over the past few years with recent revelations of how security agencies of democratic countries, such as the US, collect vast amounts of information about their citizens.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Arising from such revelations, other democratic jurisdictions have sought to update their laws to focus on and better calibrate the balance between the state's investigatory powers and the individual's right to privacy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the heart of this discussion is a desire for checks and balances that are fit for purpose for today's day and age.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Understandably, the conversation with electorates in these countries has not been easy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many people perceive the world to be in an Orwellian age, complete with fake news and the prospect of privacy intrusions by even private corporations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the absence of such a conversation in Singapore, combined with an erroneous assumption that continuing down tried and tested routes will suffice, would engender a worse outcome, even presaging a disunited population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But insofar as finding a better balance between policing and privacy, the lessons that have been taught by this TraceTogether episode inform us that they are lessons the Government would be wise not to dismiss.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In fact, this Bill also aims to enhance public trust and encourage Singaporeans to continue fighting against COVID-19 with peace of mind for the greater good.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Since the outbreak of COVID-19, more than 2.2 million people worldwide have died and over 100 million confirmed cases have been diagnosed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In Singapore, the number of confirmed cases exceeded 59,000 and the death toll is 29.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the face of this global pandemic, the Singapore Government has given top priority to the safety of our people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: All this while, our Ministries have worked together, mobilised national resources and capabilities, investing nearly $100 billion last year to support Singapore companies and workers, and established a relatively comprehensive system of testing and treatment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At present, efforts to control the pandemic have also achieved firm results.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As such, Singapore is widely praised for its COVID-19 fight.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singaporeans' lives as well as their jobs are now protected.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How many people have had to give their all to achieve this?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Outside of Singapore, we can see how COVID-19 is developing around the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What is worrying is that, even in China where the control is watertight, they have also seen a rebound of cases.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is a reminder of how fluid the situation really is.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In Singapore, vaccination is now in full swing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But with the start of the Phase 3, more people can gather in public places and hold large-scale gatherings.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We cannot rule out the possibility of another wave and must be vigilant.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Recently, there were community cases now and then.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the same time, there are news that not only has the virus not been exterminated, it has also mutated into more infectious strains.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fortunately, we are living in an age of technology.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Viruses cannot be touched or seen, but we can use the Internet and big data to track them down and isolate those who are infected.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This would be unimaginable in the last century.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Because of the advent of technology, our generation is able to better and more effectively deal with major infectious diseases globally.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Technology has given us a ray of hope so that the disasters that befell human civilisations, such as smallpox, the Plague and cholera, will not recur.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we laud the advancements of technology, there is anxiety, too, both worldwide and in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Among some communities, there are worries that big data will threaten privacy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today's amendment Bill on TraceTogether is one clear example.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: TraceTogether is critical in contact tracing within the shortest time possible to limit the spread once an infected person is identified.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The success of TraceTogether depends on all our cooperation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It was not easy to get everyone on board initially.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Apart from helping the less tech-savvy to use it, we have to consider privacy issues.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Making the coding open source and, therefore, verifiable by third parties, helped build trust in TraceTogether among the public.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, when Singaporeans later discovered that the Police could access the data for serious crime investigations, which was different from the original picture painted, it triggered a debate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Such being the case, this amendment is perhaps the most decisive move.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am confident that this will fortify the public's trust in the system.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Nevertheless, I have three clarifications to seek from the Ministers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, if this data were collected for a major crime investigation, what is the process involved and what are the controls involved during this process?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, as we move towards a digital future, more technologies and our lives will be intertwined, we cannot deny that there will be a possibility that there will be another major crisis that will affect all.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How will this Bill affect the large-scale deployment of such future technology solutions that will enhance our collective well-being?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Will it also be just limited to the investigation of these seven major crimes?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Around the world, the success or failure of the COVID-19 fight depends not so much on medical resources and technology, but on public awareness.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In countries like Europe and the US where there are strong calls for human rights, the situation seems to be more severe.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In contrast, Asian cultures that emphasise the need to abide by social rules for the sake of collective interests have made the fight against COVID-19 more effective.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the pandemic continues to worsen in most countries, entering Phase 3 means that we will enter a long-drawn war against the diseases.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government's introduction of legislation at this stage to improve contact tracing efficiency is after much consideration.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We cannot afford to let our guard down.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have to tread on thin ice and not let the efforts of the Government and society as a whole to be wasted just because of one careless moment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the fight against COVID-19, a wrong move may mean a lost war.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Think of the number of hospital wards where healthcare workers have worked overtime and the loneliness and anxiety of isolated patients and their families, the pain of being separated from those you miss.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How many students have to take part in graduation ceremonies online?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Also, how many have to bear uncertainties in their career as a result of economic changes?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the situation so fluid, some people may feel uneasy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, every life is precious and we have to use technology to fight this disease.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In Chinese mythology, Goddess Nuwa transformed her body into all that physically make up the world after she mended the sky.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Shennong died after trying out hundreds of herbs himself.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Da Yu passed by his home three times, but did not enter while managing the flood.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: All these characters in the stories shared the same spirit and that is the spirit of the greater good.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Sun Yat Sen, a great man of modern history also said that the difference between the individual and society is like the difference between the individual good and greater good.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Master Xing Yun once wrote in a Buddhist textbook that we need to elevate our love for the individual to a great compassion for all people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we interpret this from another angle, it means that mankind can and should strive to achieve the greater good and greater compassion for the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Looking back at our own history, Singapore faced great difficulties in the early days of nation building.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The prosperity and progress we have today depend to a large extent on the sacrifices and contributions of our early founders and pioneers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of them were political leaders, some representatives of Chinese businessmen, some philanthropists, some artists, some education promoters.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Their names are still familiar to us today and praised by future generations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These include Sir Stamford Raffles, founder of Singapore; Mr Lee Kuan Yew, the founding Prime Minister who fought hard for Singapore throughout his life; Mr Yusof Ishak, the first President who contributed greatly to Singapore's racial harmony; Mr Tan Kah Kee, a philanthropist; Dr Tan Tock Seng who gave medical aid to the needy; Mr Lee Kong Chian, a great educator; and also many pioneers whose names cannot be listed here.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Since the founding of Singapore, they have given their all and devoted their entire lives and wealth to promoting the political, social and economic and educational progress of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These great men have one thing in common, which is a spirit of placing the greater good over their individual good – be selfless.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Bit by bit, through their convictions, they built this dream home called Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today, I am convinced that making contributions should not be the prerogative of any segment of society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the past year, we have seen that not only have Singaporeans not been defeated by the virus, they have also shown courage and kindness.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Every frontline healthcare worker who faces the unknown with courage is also someone else's child or parent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are also food and beverage operators who are willing to give hearting-warming meals to healthcare workers despite their own financial difficulties, and volunteers who visit foreign worker dormitories despite the risk of infection to themselves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They have shown us what the Singapore spirit is.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Every man is like a drop of water.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Only when he is integrated into the sea can he see the vast expanse of the ocean.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He is like a sand integrated into the desert to form a vast desert.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When this pandemic is finally over, what will remain?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Physically tired we may be, but we will leave behind a strong sense of home and nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the face of unpredictable challenges in the future, we, as Singaporeans should consciously integrate our individual good into the greater good and uphold the spirit of "Singapore for me, me for Singapore".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I think the legislation is timely, speaks of transparency and is needed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Following my question to MHA in January, it was announced that data collected through the TraceTogether app could be used for criminal investigations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The day after, which was a Tuesday, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan provided a clarification that he had not considered the CPC when he spoke in June 2020 about the ambit of the usage of TraceTogether.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I want to say that I listened to every word that he had said and I believe him; and I want to have that stated on Hansard.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also remember Mr Pritam Singh saying in that debate that he accepts that the CPC was not in the Minister's contemplation at that time and that the remarks were made in good faith.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Again, today, presumably consistent with that position of Mr Pritam Singh in January – the consistent position being the consistent position in January – that there is no imputation of dishonesty or malice on the Minister.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I think he had quoted several groups that he had spoken to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But, in his view, there is no imputation of malice or dishonesty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And I think that is something very important to clear up because it is consistent with his initial position in January that he accepts the remark was made in good faith.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a result of my clarification, which is really clarification, which is really an answer to my question from the day earlier – I am talking about the January sitting – we are in double quick time, debating this Bill under a Certificate of Urgency.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, the fact is that we only have seven categories out of a vast number of offences in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And if you can go through the Penal Code, the Prevention of Corruption Act and the Misuse of Drugs Act, you will realise that there are many other offences outside the scope of these seven categories, including offences such as theft, battery and assault, and possession of a controlled drug which TraceTogether data cannot be used for.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here we are only carving out seven and I think this indicates that it is most certainly geared towards contact tracing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are in the midst of a pandemic and TraceTogether saves lives but we must also balance that with its ability to trace suspects for serious crimes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have been the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Chairman for Home Affairs and Law all of last term – and I know the threats we face.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I know how important it is to have the Police be given the tools to fight serious crime and I do know that the Police Force is a professional and judicious one and therefore notwithstanding the sacrifice of privacy the Bill envisions, I think on the grand scale of things, it should be supported so as to achieve the greater aim of containing a pandemic and the ancillary consequence of fighting crime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also listened intently to Mr Pritam Singh's position just now saying that, after speaking about privacy, the Workers' Party, notwithstanding, still supports the carve-out of seven offences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, supporting seven categories, it must follow that the Workers' Party accepts the sacrifice to privacy is justifiable, at least, insofar as this Bill is concerned.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because the sacrifice to privacy is a basic ingredient to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To support the ancillary purpose of fighting serious crime, it is an ingredient.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Now, what is the basis of that ingredient?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Pritam Singh calls it privacy and I would say an element of sacrifice of privacy is needed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And let me make a case for that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do want to say something in favour of Home Affairs and MinLaw and AGC and the Police, when they were looking at the seven categories of offences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do think that they were judiciously exercising self-restraint in not broadening the categories further, that is, they were trying to make the sacrifice of privacy as least painful as possible.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would have extended it to all types of drug trafficking, whether or not the offence attracted the death sentence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The ability to intervene or apprehend a suspect has, in part, to do with pre-arrest intelligence work.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: CNB may know that a known drug trafficker is going to do another drug delivery but until he is apprehended, they will not know the exact weight of the drug on him.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, it is really only when he has been apprehended with the drugs and the drugs have been weighed and found to have attracted a potential death sentence, for example, an arrest involving more than 15mg of diamorphine, that the CNB can retrospectively use the TraceTogether data of the suspect.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This, in my view, restricts CNB far too much.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What I am getting at is that I would have thought that the more efficient method in which the TraceTogether data could be used by CNB would be before the apprehension so that the source of the drug could be ascertained upstream, that is, further up the chain of trafficking.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If my guess is correct, this signals to me a judicious exercise of self-restraint, that is, the lesser the sacrifice to privacy, the better, out of respect to Singaporeans – and I dare say a sacrifice to privacy, to some extent, that the Workers' Party, is willing to accept.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I go back to this theme of balance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The overarching raison d’etre of this app is contact tracing; a lesser, ancillary consequence, is the ability to fight serious crime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And why not allow for that positive ancillary consequence if indeed it can solve crime and alleviate much distress suffered by the victims of crimes, and their families?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On balance, I think it is worth it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because for the reasons I have presented, the Bill still preserves contact tracing as the greater purpose.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Containing a pandemic through contact tracing and solving serious crimes are both – are both – virtuous exercises.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Instead, blanket assurances were given by several Ministers that the TraceTogether (TT) data would only be used for contact tracing in COVID-19 cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These blanket assurances were given from at least the middle of 2020.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Minister Vivian Balakrishnan told the House last month that he had forgotten about the Criminal Procedure Code when he gave his assurances and had sleepless nights thereafter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But the bigger question is: for all these months, why did no one in the Government step forward to correct the misrepresentation that TraceTogether was fully ringfenced for COVID-19 tracing?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, on why Police would need TraceTogether data for criminal investigations, I have some scepticism.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the TraceTogether data is likely to be incomplete and patchy.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition, people can and do turn off the Bluetooth functions on their phones.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Those using TraceTogether tokens may also not carry them around all the time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The TraceTogether system's proximity data may also have some technical limitations as to distance and time which may make records incomplete.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, it should be pointed out that some countries, like Australia, have chosen not to allow their law enforcement agencies to access information from COVID-19 contact tracing schemes for other investigations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even speaking as someone who is generally supportive of law enforcement, I believe it is important for the Government to make a convincing case for TraceTogether data use by elaborating on possible scenarios so that we can understand why TraceTogether may be pivotal to solving certain crimes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier in his speech, Minister Vivian Balakrishnan gave one scenario of a child being kidnapped.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wonder if he has other scenarios to share.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When the seven categories were announced last month, it was clear to me, at least, that the Government was making serious efforts to scope down its powers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the face of offence categories, most can agree that they are grave offences which the public would want the Police to solve.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The seven categories of offences are now listed in the Seventh Schedule of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will ensure that Members of Parliament and the public can scrutinise any change before it is law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I was expecting to see in the Seventh Schedule a listing of the exact Penal provisions being contemplated such as precisely which sections of which laws are included.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the Seventh Schedule describes the offence categories in less precise terms.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This may lead to some ambiguity and uncertainty in application.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, Category 7 is listed as, and I quote, "Any offence involving serious sexual assault such as rape or sexual assault by penetration".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The use of the phrase "such as" means that rape and sexual assault by penetration are mere examples and not exhaustive of the category of serious sexual assault.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Would this category include scenarios where the sexual assault did not involve penetration but involved, say, sexual assault of a mentally disabled victim?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Many would regard sexual assault of a mentally disabled victim as serious and, in fact, TraceTogether data might be pivotal in such cases due to the victim's reduced ability to assist in Police investigations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another example of potential ambiguity is the offence of rioting.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Rioting is defined under the Penal Code as a situation where there is an unlawful assembly of five or more persons and one member uses force or violence to pursue a common object of the assembly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If one looks at Seventh Schedule, Category 3, it seems to me that some cases of rioting may be included but not others, as it all depends on whether the injuries to the victim are of a life-threatening nature or not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Given the importance of proper classification, who will be the gatekeeper to certify whether or not a crime incident falls within the Seventh Schedule?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It should not be left to the investigator alone.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My fourth point relates to from whom the Police will extract the TraceTogether data.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill makes clear that the Police will order the production of the data, so there is no need to seek consent from the person having the data.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Referring to the parliamentary answer given by MHA to Member of Parliament Christopher de Souza on 4 January, Minister of State Desmond Tan had said that TraceTogether data would not be extracted from suspects but only from witnesses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister clarify the precise basis for distinguishing the two?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for suspects, Minister of State Tan had said that TraceTogether data would not be extracted from suspects for the purpose of security.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the Police will be able to use TraceTogether data to incriminate the suspect, then in all fairness, the TraceTogether data should be available to the defence as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Defence counsel often come onto the case some weeks after the arrest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How does the Government intend to handle this issue of justice and fairness?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, we need answers to the questions we have posed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As leaders, it is important to communicate clearly as well as in a principled manner.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If we had stated in this House that TraceTogether data is to be used only for contact tracing, then it should be so.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even if there is great benefit to be gained by using it for other purposes, even if there is fine print that allows us to do so, we should forebear.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If we want to take a different approach from what was earlier represented in this House, then we should raise the matter here for debate and convince hon Members in this House that it is necessary to change tack.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is for this reason that I welcome the introduction of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Leader of Opposition in his speech mentioned that there are quarters outside this House which ascribe a sinister motive in relation to the point as to whether the hon Minister knew from the outset that the data was to be used for other matters, apart from contact tracing, in particular, in dealing with investigation of offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is noteworthy, as the hon Leader of Opposition mentioned, was that in the hon Prime Minister's speech on the 21 April 2020, he had already stated that in relation to the digital contact tracing efforts, there could be privacy concerns.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I filed a Parliamentary Question for the sitting in June 2020.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, just looking at two points, April and June, you could already see there is a bit of a disjunct and there was an error that arose arising from the fact that while on one hand, the Prime Minister said there could be some privacy concerns, on the other, the Minister had pointed out that the data would only be used for contact tracing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I, like the hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza, looked at the chronology of the entire saga and I am convinced that this error, just like the hon Leader of Opposition said, is not an error that was intentionally made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, both the hon Leader of Opposition, Mr Pritam Singh, and the hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim, asked questions in relation to exactly when this would arise in practice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If these harms fall on your parent, your sibling, your child, and if the data from your TraceTogether token can make a difference between solving the case and leaving it unsolved, or if it means catching the criminal in days rather than in months or even years, would we not say yes?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do say yes, and this is why I support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do so for one main reason – it is in line with the current legislative policy to allow the Police access to any relevant data, no matter how personal, in their investigations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As it stands, there is no blanket privacy protection that applies across the board.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our private phone logs, our banking records, are all subject to these provisions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The need for  privacy must be weighed against the demands of justice, and the need to protect the safety and security of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We are by no means unique in taking this stance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I made mention last month in this House that there is parity between the positions taken in Singapore and the European Union through its General Data Protection Regulations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: An easy way out of this decision, it would be to say that TraceTogether and SafeEntry, taken together, is an aberration – if it had not existed, what would the Police do?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Police have solved crimes before TraceTogether and SafeEntry, and will do so after the programme has been stood down.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, why do we feel it needs this?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It would indeed be the easier route – just keep to the original promise, forget about the data and pretend we never had it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But the fact remains that this is not a hypothetical armchair philosophy question.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have real crimes, real lives at stake.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is morally indefensible to shut our eyes to the answer when knowing it would make a difference in cracking a serious crime case and bringing the culprit to face justice and, possibly, save other lives from being victims of serious crime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is not a crude utilitarian trampling of principles for a greater good.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is, in fact, the principle from which all Police powers come – the demand for justice, the right to be protected from evil and harm.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To those people who are troubled because they received this raft of conspiracy messages, saying that, "Oh, the Police has no system to protect data and they use it for all kinds of issues"; let me just say it for myself as a criminal lawyer for the past 25 years and a former police officer before that, that I know personally how seriously the Police deals with issues of misuse of data.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I know of cases, some of them were cases where I represented the ex-officer, where there was misuse of data, and the Police officers concerned were prosecuted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, there is a system and I would want to share my own experience with those who are troubled by these conspiracy messages.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A more difficult question – and that was posed by the hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza – is why then limit this access to serious crimes as defined under the Bill, given the state of law at this point?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He spoke about the need to extend it to cover other classes of drug offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With respect, this question ignores the facts and circumstances that have led us to this point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As hon Members are already familiar with the background, I will desist from recounting it again in my speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do appreciate the hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim's point about the fact that they are not defined in terms of cross-reference to provisions but there is already description of the serious crimes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Using the general principles of interpretation, one would get to know what is parliamentary intention.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is far worse than a year ago – the mutating virus has variants which are more infectious and lethal, more than 2 million dead across the world, a reporter in tears on "live" TV as she visited hospitals where patients are dying from lack of proper healthcare, students in a university ringfenced by metal fences to regulate visitor movements and keep them safe.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This quick escalation can happen in Singapore if we were to lose our cohesion resulting in our healthcare resources being overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even the vaccine is not a magic bullet.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All we have is our very human responses – our responsibility to each other, our own recognition of our vulnerabilities, our hopes and our better selves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: TraceTogether and SafeEntry, collectively, is a tool to help us in this pandemic and we need it in this new and present threat.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also a tool to help us against the old evils of human depravity, greed and lust.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is no reason why it cannot do both.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even if one contact were traced through which one serious crime is solved or one serious crime is prevented, it would be worthwhile.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And we just need one reason to support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In closing, I would like to refer to the hon Leader of Opposition's point about the future and how we should regulate data in the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would suggest, especially, in the context of the present crisis and the efforts being expended to contain the threat of COVID-19, we should also be looking at the future when we have to contain another crisis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In that kind of scenario, what would we want to be as Members in this House?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Should we just be ambassadors of our people, just conveying what this group of people have expressed, or that group of people have expressed?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Or would it be necessary that we bear the responsibility as leaders to move our people, to say, "This is a crisis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Look at the outcome." We must have the courage to move our people in one direction to overcome the crisis together.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And that to me would be a big lesson for the future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I would just like to pick up on a point the hon Member made about the easy way out being to just proceed as originally assured by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, the Government obviously had to weigh the implications of going ahead, proceeding as assured by the Minister and the Government or introducing the exemptions for serious crimes at this point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In those circumstances, the critical issue in my mind is to determine which way do you go, where do you fall.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I would suggest that it is not a question of armchair philosophy or trying to defend something that is morally indefensible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because, as a society, we have rules in very different situations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The hon Member is a criminal lawyer of some repute.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Outside this Chamber, I think people like me would be going to him for advice on criminal matters.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I could be representing a criminal who could have admitted to me that he committed an offence but my instructions is to plead not guilty for him in Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And that puts a lot of pressure on criminal lawyers, as the Member would know.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: You do not take up the case; you drop the brief.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Or you make sure you follow those instructions to a hilt because if you do not, you have committed some offences vis-a-vis the Legal Profession Act and you have breached client confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not suggesting an equivalence to TraceTogether.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But, effectively, that lawyer is a walking TraceTogether token.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As far as society is concerned, that is a trade-off.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And insofar as how a conviction or a decision to prosecute turns on TraceTogether data, it is not exactly hypothetical.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The hon Member Mr Christoper de Souza has talked about expanding actually the scope of Misuse of Drugs Act, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I just wanted to verbalise my views on the points that hon Member Mr Murali made about, suggesting that this is an easy way out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not think that is the nub of the issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think it is far deeper than that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I think, Sir, I just have one clarification for Member Mr Murali.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: If I heard him correctly, during his speech, he said he is comforted by the fact that the Bill states that the TraceTogether data would only be accessed when there is clear and pressing need.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: One, that TraceTogether or TT data is not and will never be used for anything other than contact tracing, as per their earlier assurances.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Or two, that the TT data may be used for criminal investigations in some circumstances.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I thought the second scenario would be less likely.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I shared with a colleague ahead of that day's Sitting that I did not think the Government would use TT data for non-contact tracing purposes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
