text: It will cause a public outcry as it would inviolate TT's privacy policy and what the Government had been saying about TT's privacy protection so far.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More damagingly, it could lead to a lower adoption rate of TT, which would in turn hinder our battle against the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As it turned out, option two was closer to reality.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In response to my supplementary question that day, the Minister of State clarified that other than for the purpose of criminal investigations and protecting public safety and security, TT data is to be used only for contact tracing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The next day, on 5 January, the Minister for Foreign Affairs made a clarification, following a lot of unease expressed by Singaporeans about the previous day's revelations, where he stated that the use of TT data would be restricted to serious crimes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Why did the Government choose the make this revelation only on 4 January, more than nine months after TT was launched?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On 8 June 2020, the Minister for Foreign Affairs had stated in a press conference that TT data is "only used for contact tracing".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While the Minister has since admitted that he had not thought of the CPC at that time – and I appreciate his explanation – why did anyone in Government not come out sooner to correct this statement?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many Singaporeans downloaded the TT app and collected the TT token in large numbers, in part, because they trusted the Government's assurances of privacy and limitation of use.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This unfortunate sequence of events may make many Singaporeans more wary of taking Government's statements at face value.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some may now adopt Ronald Reagan's adage, "Trust, but verify".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We may now have an 80% adoption rate for TT but we should not rest on our laurels and become complacent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, the more people use TT, the more effective contact tracing will be.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should always aim for maximum adoption and usage and minimise any obstacles to adoption.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, privacy fears or poor app performance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are many ways that TT can be disabled.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There is even a pause function within the TT app itself.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Suffice to say, one does not need to be a rocket scientist to figure out how to legally disable the TT app or token.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With the 4 January revelation, many people who anticipate engaging and even minor misdemeanours may choose to disable TT just to avoid detection.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some might even do so to avoid being called as a witness in a Court case.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Others may do so as matter of principle or because of their lack of trust in the Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All these might add up to a not-so-insignificant proportion of our population.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We may think that these people are holding out on TT for unjustifiable reasons, especially since the seven serious crimes have already been scoped in.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, we cannot control every action that individuals make with their electronic devices.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The net result may be a lower than desired usage of TT which will hamper our contact tracing efforts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government does not want to constrain itself by committing to "never use TT data for crime fighting".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, is the potential cost of slower containment of the community's spread of COVID-19 worth it?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Put another way, if the COVID-19 situation were to take a turn for the worse, overwhelming our healthcare system, will the Police still use TraceTogether data if it inevitably suppresses the adoption rate and hinders contact tracing efforts?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Mr Murali has said that it is worth using contact tracing data even if one serious crime is solved.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On the flip side, is it worth it if even one COVID-19 cluster goes undetected because a few people deactivated the TT app out of privacy concerns?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, I hope the Government and the Police will now consider this question carefully in deciding how often and to what extent it uses the broad powers conferred on it by section 20 of the CPC and this Bill.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Since its launch, how many times have the Police used SafeEntry data for investigations and how many of these investigations were outside the scope of the seven serious crimes in the Seventh Schedule?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The pandemic may last another four to five years, as Minister Lawrence Wong has recently alluded to.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In an even more pessimistic scenario, COVID-19 may never be fully eradicated but will become endemic in our population.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If this happens, will these digital contact tracing systems ever be stood down?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What are the criteria that will be used to determine this?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: He said that he obtained the information from a Government statement.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many Singaporeans recognise the importance of contact tracing in our quest to keep Singaporeans and Singapore safe during this COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the clarification that TraceTogether data can be accessed by the Police under the Criminal Procedure Code, I, like many, have received feedback from residents expressing disappointment and concerns.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This change from the earlier assurances given that TraceTogether data would only be used for COVID-19 contact tracing purposes is something that has caused some disquiet.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I can understand that many are upset because many had collected the token or downloaded the app on this assurance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I do want to make this point about looking at the TraceTogether solution and what the Minister has shared earlier with regards to the design decisions on TraceTogether.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think that it is clear that TraceTogether is purpose-built with the singular purpose for COVID-19 contact tracing to prevent a situation of the spread of COVID-19 and with privacy protection central to that design.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: First, TraceTogether utilises, as many have said, Bluetooth exchanges to capture proximity of who has been close to you.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This token or app does not use GPS capabilities and hence does not capture location information.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This data is also captured and stored on the token or the app and not on the server.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The scope of the TraceTogether solution has been very singular in that purpose of design.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The fact is that data is deleted after 25 days – based on what the Minister had shared – based on medical advice of the time required for contact tracing data, if required, and that it is deleted after that time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If you think about it from a design purpose, it is clear.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I think the important question now for all of us, in front of us now, is: do we restrict the use of that contact tracing data?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This Bill seeks to limit the use of personal data collected for COVID-19 through digital contact tracing solutions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Despite the intent of the Bill to limit the use of personal contact tracing data for the specified seven categories of serious crimes, some have asked if we should even allow access – and this discussion has been happening outside of this Chamber as well – and use of data for any other purpose as there was assurance given earlier that the information was for the sole purpose of COVID-19 contact tracing in the event that there is an infection.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many have also pointed out that there is no need for the data from TraceTogether to be used as there are other sources of more intelligent data and information available from other smarter devices.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These include close-circuit TVs installed in buildings, elevators, along our streets, in-vehicle cameras, and GPS devices including smartphones, just to name a few.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With data from these devices, is there really a need for the data from TraceTogether?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Given the earlier assurance and the mistake made – I think the Leader of the Opposition and Mr Murali have also pointed this out, and I think we have had a discussion – I actually ask this question of myself: would be be an easier decision not to allow the use of the TraceTogether data for any other purpose?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Easier in the sense that because of what people are feeling and the angst that some are feeling.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But then I ask myself again: is it the right decision?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we take the position not to allow access to TraceTogether data for the purpose of police investigation when a serious crime is committed, what it would mean is that even if the data from the TraceTogether token or app could help in the investigation, even if there is a remote possibility, the Police cannot access the data.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Minister gave the example of someone being kidnapped.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I actually wrote that down for my speech too.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the event that someone was kidnapped – I had this discussion with a resident – if that happened, and if TraceTogether data, in the remotest possibility, was the only available data that could provide a lead in expediting investigations in that situation, what it would mean is that the data cannot be accessed if we did not have this discussion and we did not agree on this Bill.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Knowing the implications of this, I ask myself again: would it be the right decision for us to agree that the data cannot be used even if it could save a life?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I come to this point that – I think there is some talk about whether it is convenient or easy for the Police.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Are we making it easier for the Police to investigate rather than using other data?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think we all agree this is not about convenience.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is really about aiding and helping in investigations of serious crimes – matters that involve, in some cases, life and death.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I know this is somewhat a practical question but can the Minister share what will be done to prevent such misuse?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Now that it could be used for criminal investigations of serious crimes, I think there are some voters who may be worried that their token or their app might be misused by someone else.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we protect data privacy – and I think the reason for this Bill is that we recognise that privacy is important – we must make the right decision to protect and keep Singapore and Singaporeans safe and secure.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Before I end, I do want to touch on this point because I think there were some discussions about whether this Bill will cause lower take up rates of TraceTogether.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think that is the purpose of why we are having this conversation in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is to help Singaporeans understand why this balance needs to be made.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think to some extent I trust that Singaporeans, with the right information and understanding, will move in the right direction and support the use of digital solutions to help with contact tracing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We have seen that of Singaporeans since COVID-19 started till now.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We have seen how Singaporeans have stepped up.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There have been so many restrictions made on everybody's lives but everyone has played their part.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think it is important we have this conversation so that Singaporeans can make the right decision to continue to move forward together, to keep everyone safe.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Public trust in the Government is the cornerstone of Singapore's political system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our people's trust in the Government enabled the first-generation leaders to transform Singapore from a third-world country to a first-world country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This very same trust enabled the Government to combat and curtail the SARS crisis in 2003 and the H1N1 crisis in 2009.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it would be remiss of me not to state that our contact tracing programmes intrude extensively upon our people's privacy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SafeEntry collects an individual's NRIC, contact number, their location, whenever they enter a building and even how long an individual stays in a location, while TraceTogether collects who that individual was in close proximity to and for how long.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The two programmes together allow the Government to easily create a map where an individual goes and who he associates with.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans have long accepted some erosion over their civil rights and by extension their privacy, in order to ensure public safety.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, when the Government announced the TraceTogether token in June 2020, there was a public backlash against TraceTogether.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over concerns that TraceTogether will invade their privacy and the collected data will be used for non-contact tracing purposes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is because of this broken trust that we are gathered here today debating a Bill that has to be passed under a Certificate of Urgency, which means that all the three Readings of the Bill would have to be done in this Parliament Sitting and there will be little time to consider its implications carefully.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Actually, to start repairing the broken trust, the Government must first answer questions about the follow-up process around this episode.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like when did the Police first access the TT data?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When the TT data was accessed, did the Police consider that they will be breaking the promise that the Government gave to not use the TT data for anything other than for the purposes of fighting the pandemic?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has the TT data been accessed only once as Minister Balakrishnan has stated in the previous sitting, or more than once?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If more than once, how many cases exactly has the Police actually accessed?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When was Cabinet first informed that TT data was accessed in a direct breach of the promise they gave?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Did Cabinet then gave instructions to the Police not to access TT data in light of their repeated and public promises?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These five questions apply with equal force to the data collector under the SafeEntry programme, which has so far attracted less attention.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the PSP Secretary-General, Dr Tan Cheng Bock has stated, backtracking is not good politics and it erodes the confidence and social compact of our citizens in our political institutions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At this point in the pandemic, the last thing we need is for our citizens to lose faith in the Government and start second-guessing the Government's motives whenever in announces new measures to control the COVID-19 virus, especially when other countries around the world are experiencing new outbreaks.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government is compromising public health and public trust for some benefit in public safety by passing this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Public trust in TraceTogether has been eroded by this broken promise.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What I found when speaking to residents is that they are now leaving their TraceTogether tokens at home when they go out.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And some are now refusing to use TraceTogether altogether.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will compromise the effectiveness of contact tracing efforts, and this is exceptionally dangerous in light of the uptick in community cases since Singapore's move into Phase Three.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SPF has already broad powers to assess documents, things, data, computers and even decryption data under the Criminal Procedure Code for the purposes of investigating crimes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides I find it quite unbelievable that such criminals would carry their TraceTogether tokens when committing such crimes, especially now that the Government has announced the TT data is accessible by the Police.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's biggest priority now should be to fight the COVID-19 pandemic and persuade as many people as possible to use TraceTogether.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This must be the call and primary purpose.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Any other purpose that compromises on this primary purpose and cause people to reconsider using TraceTogether must be set aside.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have thought of supporting it with some changes, but to trade off public trust in public health measures, which must be of utmost priority in a pandemic crisis, for public safety, is too much to give for us, after much consideration.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the complete ring-fencing of contact tracing data, keeping it solely for public health objective, is not unprecedented.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must also keep in mind that the COVID-19 pandemic will neither be the first nor the last pandemic that our country will have to deal with.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I, too, have my reservations on this Bill, but it largely has to do with the limits its placing on the powers of the Police to obtain information under the CPC.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And I think one of the points that we cannot trivialise, is how difficult Police investigations are and how difficult the process of finding the truth can be as well, even if matters were to go to Court.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore, we have a low crime rate and most Singaporeans go about their daily lives without fear of crime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: An important reason for this is that we have effective law enforcement by the Police.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is one of the smallest in the developed world and even amongst our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, despite the small Police Force, they have been effective at keeping the crime rates low.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is in part because it has strong support from the population.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And people make reports whenever they see anything amiss.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For Members of Parliament, you know this, almost every other thing ends up in a Police report; whether it is a neighbour dispute, complaint about noise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When a crime happens, Police have to piece together what happened.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The crime scene is not going to the tell the Police the story.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If they are lucky, they will have eyewitnesses who can identify the accused, get confessions and close the case.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But what if they do not have ready eyewitnesses?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What if they have people who were there but who did not see things but who may be able to give information or device?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are all different situations you may find yourself in after a crime has happened.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Police have a wide variety of investigated methods, that is, old-fashioned style investigations, maybe like Sherlock Holmes – you look for clues, you piece together, you draw inferences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But while those make good stories, they do not help you solve a large number of crimes that take place regularly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, Police use data, they use technology, they find corroborating evidence from as many sources as possible to try and understand what happened.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even after Police work is done and the suspect is found, a trial may be necessary if the suspect does not plead guilty and where evidence gathered by the Police and investigators are put to rigorous testing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a lawyer, I take part in trials and I can tell you, the truth is not always straightforward.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There will be competing versions of narratives and the Judge sitting there has to decide who is telling the truth.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The more information and data you have, the better you will be able to piece the story together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And the standard for proving guilt is beyond reasonable doubt.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, it is a very high threshold you have to take before you can establish someone has done something wrong.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The general rules of evidence, certainly in civil proceedings is, you have a duty to disclose all evidence that is not privileged, even if it goes against your client's case.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is because your primary obligation is with the Court, to help the Court find the truth.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even in criminal proceedings, there are obligations on prosecutors to disclose evidence that may go towards showing the person is not guilty.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: All this is there because we want the Courts to have the best available information to arrive at the truth.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, generally, the rules and the society that we live in has this presumption that the Court has to have access to all available information.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And, of course, for the information to get to the Court, it must first be gathered, in this case, by the Police.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, against this backdrop of the manpower crunch, Police have regularly kept up with the latest policing methods, using technology wherever possible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One obvious example is the use of CCTVs, which are now there at the ground floor lift lobbies and staircases to HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is obviously a trade-off in privacy, but I think Singaporeans have generally been comfortable with this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They trust the Police; they cooperate with the Police.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I always find more requests for more CCTVs, not less.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In fact, with most of my residents, the kinds of things they ask surveillance for usually gets rejected but this includes dealing loanshark harassment, littering, inconsiderate neighbourly behaviours, noise nuisance, speeding, traffic offences and parking offences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Police have done a very good job of dealing with serious crime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Minor crime is obviously not prioritised but this is what causes the most nuisance amongst many of our residents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And even in these situations, people are always ready to trade off privacy for a fast resolution to issues.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: People understand that Police have limited resources and they are generally supportive unmanned surveillance methods.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is not this autonomous pilot scene where everyone goes, what you are doing or is it going to retrace your story.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The only information TraceTogether has is who is near you at that point in time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is obviously very useful in contact tracing because you may not know all the people you are in close contact with over a two-week period.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But for this very reason, it can also be helpful if you are trying to solve "who done it", a mystery of what happened here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Let us say, obviously, in a case of murder, it is very clear cut.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The victim cannot speak; the victim is dead.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: You may be able to infer from that device who was in close proximity at the time of the event.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What about cases where you cannot see the victim.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Your token is here but you did not see what happened but you were at the location.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: By the time the Police come, the people involved in the fight had disappeared.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If that fight is not serious, then, that is going to be one of those potential unsolved crimes – people disappeared, not serious enough to investigate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But if they could use TraceTogether data to find out who did it, then that may be another solved crime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Would you want your TraceTogether data to assist in Police investigations with that situation?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Likewise, if someone was hauled up, being interrogated for a crime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And if he were to say, "Oh, yeah, I was in the coffeeshop and I think the Member of Parliament was there, maybe Member of Parliament so and so".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Then, if he was not close proximity, he maybe blindsided, cannot remember, you can check the TraceTogether data as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The key point about TraceTogether is that it is useful to place you together with a stranger and placing a person is an important part of the solving the mystery of the crime – who done it? where was he at the time it happened?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do not see any principled reason why this data should not be relied on by Police.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I also have reservations on things that are excluded.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These acts are not serious under the current legislation but would you want the Police to use all data available to solve these crimes?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If you were a victim, if one of your family members was a victim, would you want Police to use all available data?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If you were wrongly accused, would you want the Police to use this data to show you were somewhere else the time it happened?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But that cannot be done now, unless it is a serious crime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: SafeEntry would show what time you entered a place and maybe what time you left if you had checked out.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I know that at many places, they monitor you checking in but they do not monitor you checking out.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is just one more clue to help put the whole picture together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If used in conjunction with TraceTogether, it may show when you went and it may show when you left, if you can remember where you went to and the Police can find someone else who was there at that point in time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To me, what SafeEntry does, is similar to what visitor logs at condominiums and so on, may have done.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, we accept that people who maintain properties can keep entrances of visitors when they come and go.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And this is often used in, both in civil cases as well as in criminal cases to find out whether a person was at a particular location, at a particular point in time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To me, SafeEntry is a far more sophisticated visitor log far, more accurate, and the fact that its use is being limited is actually a concern because, again what you are saying is, no, no, you cannot see the whole picture, you just have to work with this limit of information.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To me, in identifying how a crime happened, who was there, these are not straightforward processes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And for those who do trials, there is plenty of uncertainty involved in all these things.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The more information you have, the better you can test the truth or falsity of a person's story.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, if we want to keep COVID-19 in control, we need to use TraceTogether.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A person does not have to remember where they were the last 14 days.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They do not have to remember exactly how much time they spent at each place nor do you have to do individual interviews for each and every person.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, to me, it goes without saying that TraceTogether is necessary for this fight.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Is it a huge invasion of your privacy?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my view, the fact that TraceTogether can be used to solve crimes, it may help exonerate innocent people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To, me, that is one more reason to use it, rather than to be afraid of using it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, it is our duty as Members of this House to be role models as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So I think it is important for us not just to reiterate or echo fears that are outside but explain to people whether there is a proper basis for their fears or whether these fears may be overblown and the important considerations, the benefits of using this outweigh, whatever fears we may have.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Because ultimately, when we use TraceTogether, the more of us that use it, the better we can solve the community spread of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I also hope the better we can solve crime.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The following months saw governments across the world pushed into doing the same, changing our lives and livelihoods in substantial ways for the safety of our citizens.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, the situation is largely under control.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thanks to the sacrifices of our frontline workers, work by our Government and Civil Service, and the civic mindedness of our citizens in complying with regulations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But the community cases remind us that the COVID-19 curve has only been flattened, and not quashed.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With every report of a new case, what swiftly follows are assurances that the close contacts are being identified and quarantined, the capabilities of our contact tracing team on full display.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is the first time that a database of Bluetooth data that can tell who we are with, and for approximately how long, is recorded and accessible by the Government under specified conditions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My worry is that despite the utility and practicality of TT, the cost of going beyond the initial promise of what the TT data can be used for may drive away those who are skeptical of the assurances which this Bill is actually seeking to provide.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To move forward together, I hope for a focus on building trust and gaining confidence for the programme.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And, in this respect I have some clarifications to raise, and assurances I hope to seek.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These fall into three broad categories: first, transparency in the technology; second, transparency in the projected life cycle and use; and third, transparency in the process of using TT data in investigations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When the TT programme first started, the Government gave public access to the technology behind it.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The programme's base code, Opentrace, is open source.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I received an email from a young resident of mine seeking clarification on the continued commitment in making Opentrace, open source.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As of 10 January, the Opentrace Github repository for Android was updated close to 10 months prior.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the app on Play Store was updated on 7 December.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This suggests that the version listed on the Github repository, is not the same version as that which was on the application.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are also no opensource licences listed and the terms of use and distribution should be outlined in the repository itself.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some suggestions for consideration are: to ensure that the Github repository is updated within a reasonable time when there are application updates that have been rolled out; to update the Opentrace repository with opensource licences; to publish brief transparency reports on perhaps a bi-annual basis that will help the public understand how the data is being used, provided that the release of such data will not disrupt any investigations; and to reaffirm the commitment that TT data will always be stored on the user's device, only shared with the Government when the user takes action to upload the data and can be deleted at the request of the user.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On my second point, there are several stages in the investigation and criminal prosecution process.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Generally, when the Police have been informed of a possible offence, an investigation is initiated.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The investigation officers or IOs meet with the prosecutors in the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC).

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The DPPs will decide on the actual charge to proceed with, subject to their own internal procedures and approval structures, as well as whether sufficient evidence has been collected.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The person under investigation or arrest will then appear in Court to be formally charged.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But some investigations do not conclude with the person investigated being charged for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For cases that proceed to prosecution, at the stage of criminal investigations, our IOs would likely have an idea of the range of offences which could apply.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But the final charge may not be set out until much later.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even then, during trial, charges may be amended or dropped.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I note section 82(7), I would also like to seek confirmation whether an individual will be able to meaningfully offer both his TT and SafeEntry data as evidence.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the event one is being investigated for a serious offence but claims innocence, can such individual volunteer and access personal contact tracing data, noting the possible privacy concerns of others, as that individual's personal contact tracing data may involve the data of others who were around the individual at a particular time.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And, finally, for example, in a case of sexual assault, it can be a very traumatic experience for victims.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Cases do go unreported and some take a very long time before they come to light.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would appreciate if the Government could please share some of its considerations in this regard.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is speculation circulating, and the only way to combat this speculation is with clarity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Specifically, I would like to request for clarity on the life cycle of the programme.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: People want to have an understanding and assurance on how long the programme will last, that it will continue to remain opt-in, under what conditions that may change and when it would be laid to rest.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of course, it is impossible for us to give a fixed date for when the TT programme can be terminated as it is still unclear how long COVID-19 will last and even more uncertain what its impact may be on society at large.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, it is possible for us to take a condition-based approach in detailing the life cycle of the TT programme, a way of specifying the conditions that will prompt a significant change in our present use of the TT app and device.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is so Singaporeans are prepared in advance for any changes in the TT programme as the conditions and parameters for this would have already been specified.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we are dealing with unprecedented challenges and we recognise that things change very quickly, such an open approach will help engender trust.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In closing, Mr Speaker, Sir, at the heart of it, I, along with many Singaporeans, believe in the importance of contact tracing and the utility of the TT programme.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have read a number of concerns and confusion over the past month and I do feel bad for the engineers and teams behind the programme because I genuinely believe they were doing the best they can, all the while working in the heat of a crisis under immense pressure.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also appreciate the difficult position that we are debating today and the Minister's candour.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that some of the above clarifications can be addressed.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding the above, Mr Speaker, Sir, I believe that the Bill reflects a practical position and compromise, and express my support.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, many countries around the world are currently dealing with major outbreaks.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In Singapore, we have a multi-layered strategy to keep ourselves safe, for as long as possible.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But, crucially, every single layer in this strategy rests on trust between the Government and its people.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Safe distancing, wearing of masks, complying with group size limits, keeping at all the Safe Management Measures and resisting fatigue and complacency – we can only do this if there is trust between the Government and its people.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Getting as much of our population vaccinated as possible, allaying concerns, countering misinformation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These too require trust between the Government and its people.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And participating voluntarily in a national contact tracing scheme like TraceTogether certainly requires that same trust.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In short, trust is the lynchpin in every layer of our multi-layered strategy to stay safe in a COVID-19 world.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Some have pointed out that other technological applications that are so prevalent in our lives today have far broader terms of use regarding our personal data.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But that is really not the point, and in any case, the trust between Government and its people is a completely different matter.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I was, therefore, very concerned about how Singaporeans would take to the Government's clarifications on this matter last month, and to the proposed amendments before us today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this respect, I was relieved to observe that, in general, in fact, the level of participation and the desire to participate in TraceTogether had actually remained high.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, many of my residents have been anxious to collect their tokens and were asking me when stock at the Community Club would be replenished – happy to know that stock has arrived.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Other residents pointed out to me that the amendments actually limit Police access to a much narrower scope than what the Criminal Procedure Code provides for.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, ultimately, it was really a dilemma for me.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On the one hand, the need to jealously safeguard trust in the interest of public health.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.11 pm until 4.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are proud of the work that they do in keeping all of us safe.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They are not known to abuse their authority and they have always used their investigative powers diligently.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They are the reason they walk our streets safely and our children play freely.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: After all, public safety and public health are of equal importance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, I can empathise with the reasons for the unhappiness.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The abrupt change in the terms concerning personal data usage is upsetting for many.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this pandemic, the people have entrusted their personal data for an important purpose.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This breakdown in communication could have been avoided.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If more time was spent engaging various stakeholders and examining the communication strategy for loopholes, we could have avoided the current situation that we are in.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But with the urgency due to the raging pandemic last year, I can fully understand that things developed quickly and this unfortunately led to incomplete and inaccurate information being disseminated to the public.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The communication process could indeed have been better managed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Coming back to the use of TraceTogether for Police investigations, I think it bears repeating that Singapore is ranked top for personal safety.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is according to the most recently available 2019 Safe Cities Index published by the Economist Intelligence Unit.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have our Police and security agencies to thank for this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just as it is with combating COVID-19, we must not take our safety and security for granted.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore may be safe, but it is not crime-free.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In 2019 alone, 155 serious crimes were recorded, including some violent ones, and in recent months, resurfacing of cold cases, a small number of which were horrific crimes involving suspected murder and rape that remain unsolved till today due to the lack of sufficient evidence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Indeed, therefore, access to information is key to the resolution of any crime.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Police need evidence and the sooner the better, the more complete the better.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To leave no stone unturned is perhaps the unspoken operational motto that guides exemplary police forces around the world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This helps them to protect civilians' safety and security.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, it strikes me as counterintuitive to deliberately place restrictions on the Police on their access to information that could be helpful in the course of the investigation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It would be akin to walking past a bloody knife and ignoring it completely.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While it may be rare that TraceTogether data could produce conclusive evidence for every single investigation that it is used for, sometimes you just need one small jigsaw piece to complete the puzzle.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are crimes that might not at the current moment be classified as serious crimes but have the potential to escalate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have seen in various cases, not just locally but internationally, that stalking can give rise to more serious crimes such as sexual assault or even murder and kidnapping.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If you have to commit a crime, do not bring along your TraceTogether token then.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Most are opportunistic: molest, pickpocketing, even assaults are sometimes committed on impulse and are not so much pre-planned.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These situations will benefit from the use of TT data in investigations as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many also tend to look at the use of TT data, in the most recent conversations, solely for the Police to establish guilt or to trace where you have been.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us not forget that in the entire process of investigation – all the way from Police until it makes its way to Court – it is also equally important that evidence is available to prove innocence, not just guilt.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Whatever the gravity of the crime, any miscarriage of justice, whether for a minor crime or a serious crime, weighs equally on the person.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some may of course argue that it is the Police's responsibility to seek out evidence via other channels that have always been available – a plethora of sources of information – and therefore the Police need not use TraceTogether.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That might be true to a certain extent but if it makes it more efficient, if it solves a crime, it saves a life and it safeguards security in our society, it upholds justice, I fail to comprehend why they should be denied access to any tool that would allow them to do so.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Time is of the essence in any investigation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the years, new technology has been consistently introduced and existing ones also enhanced to aid our Police, to improve the quality and speed of investigations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Police are therefore able to review many cases with conclusive results.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I therefore fear that if we start introducing restrictions to Police investigative prerogatives, this will set a precedence for future technology where then, there is an expectation that applicable scenarios must be spelt out in full.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will then seriously impact the capability of not only the Police but other security agencies and the Government because they would have to overcome a huge amount of red tape just to get evidence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On a wider scale, it is also imperative that we get our priorities right.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Data privacy is important, I think it is universally acknowledged – but so is safety, security, life, preservation of life, both in health as well as in safety.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In other countries, the limitation of capability and access to information seriously impacted the management of many governments on the pandemic itself.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some governments have had to seek approval to declare a state of emergency or to introduce measures just to control COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even when powers are accorded, they are inadequate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There have been mention of other jurisdictions where contact tracing have been limited.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not because of some noble ideal but because no one is taking it seriously.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These measures are not so much a noble ideal in protecting the privacy but to encourage them to protect their lives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singaporeans amidst this pandemic have been responsible, cooperative and with a mind on the greater social good.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Had all the cards been laid on the table from the very beginning, perhaps we would not even be having this debate today.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I come back to the point I made three times in this speech – that I am uncomfortable with Police access to any information that will be helpful to keep our society safe.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because even if the Police is allowed to use the data, it does not mean that they use it callously.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The hon Member Mr Murali, from his experience, has also indicated that the Police take the use of evidence and personal data very seriously.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not something that they throw about willy-nilly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If there is an infraction, there is a misuse of the data, it is punished, action is taken.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are in the midst of a pandemic.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We use to build our resilience against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It helps to keep all of us healthy and safe, and it is crucial in reducing community cases.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the past months have demonstrated, we are far from being immune to COVID-19 resurgence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have seen that in many other countries.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Any refusal to participate in contract tracing will impede our efforts and turn us back from the gains we have made in the last year.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore we must stay rational in this process.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I emphasise again that I am uncomfortable with the limits upon our Police capability to solve crime and to keep us safe and also to prove innocence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This must therefore not set the precedence for future data access for new technology when it comes to issues of public safety.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Stability, safety, security and human lives are at stake, pandemic or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My visit to our recently set up swab centres in Pasir Ris gives me every confidence that we have and will continue to take appropriate measures to respond quickly and effectively to curtail the spread of this virus.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The pandemic has also expedited our use of digital tools such as the contact tracing app.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This has enabled us to perform contact tracing more efficiently and reducing the need for laborious manual process.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Personally, I have had two meetings that were cancelled because members were placed on SHN based on TT information that they were in contact with a suspected case.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I am glad that this information was made available and has protected me and my family from potential exposure to the virus, especially when I have elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is fantastic to see how, as a community, we have managed to leverage on technology to combat this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is not far-fetched to state that every single one of us is responsible for the effectiveness of TraceTogether, and we must continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With it, we can quickly trace anyone who has been exposed to the virus, and take the necessary steps to quarantine and prevent them from infecting others.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Time is of the essence for contact tracing to be effective.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Only through the concerted and responsible use of TT will we be able to do contact tracing quickly, and slow down the spread of virus.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In true digital "gotong-royong" fashion, all of us helping each other out, serving the greater good of society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Safety, security and justice are societal values that we all agree are important.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Collectively, we work hard to ensure that we are able to uphold these qualities within our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of us would even say that these qualities should never be compromised.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Singapore Police Force plays a fundamental role in ensuring that we continue to enjoy a safe, secure and just Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must continue to support our Police Force in its efforts to prevent, deter and detect crime.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And our men in blue must be suitably equipped to do their duties effectively.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We all believe and trust the Police Force to leave no stones unturned when it comes to the safety and security of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And that they would bring about swift justice to those who have broken our laws.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Criminal Procedure Code or CPC has allowed our Police Force powers to obtain information as part of their investigations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should we be setting a precedent of precluding certain sets of information to be used by law enforcement agencies in their pursuit of justice?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What this potentially means is that information that may assist in investigations cannot be used by the Police.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And conversely, it may mean that an innocent man is not able to use information from TT as an alibi to prove his innocence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From a data use point of view, the preclusion of certain sources of data seems to only make the jobs of our men in blue much more difficult.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And yet we fundamentally agree that their work to preserve our safety and security, and facilitate the enactment of justice are important features of our society which we must uphold.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The recent case of the 16-year-old radical detained under ISA reiterates the fact that we can never take our safety and security for granted and, hence, should we not allow our Police Force every information to help them achieve their mission?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moreover, when we start to preclude sets of information from being used by our Police Force, we set a dangerous precedent for future preclusions of access to data.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we undergo further digitalisation of our nation, we will create even more technologies and sets of data or information that we are only beginning to discover its benefits and applications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are we really ready to say that we will not allow some of these future technological benefits and applications to be used by our law enforcement agencies in our pursuit for a safe, secure and more just Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It must be reiterated that CPC only allows for such information to be used for criminal investigations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is not in the public’s interest to deny our law enforcement agencies access to such data if it can be used to serve the public good.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond the arguments of protection of personal privacy, should not safety, security and pursuit of justice for our society take precedence and be prioritised?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, when a person is wrongfully accused of molestation, would the individual not be able to use location data to provide an alibi as evidence that he is innocent?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Or in the search for a criminal witness, would the victim not be able to ask for help from strangers in the vicinity?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For child molestation cases, from the perspective of parents, like many of us here, TT data may be able to assist investigations in such cases.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is it not our social responsibility towards the victim's families to enable police to use data and any possible resources that can help the victims and families find justice?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a society, we still uphold societal values such as security, prosperity and justice which should never be compromised.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the pursuit of justice, we are confident in that the law enforcement agencies will conduct thorough investigations and our Police Force will remain as a pillar of safety and peace that we have enjoyed all this time.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have just embarked on a digitalisation journey and there are many more new things that we need to know to ensure that the law enforcement agencies can continue to move ahead.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the moment, once we have become aware of how TT data can assist police investigations, we cannot deliberately disregard, obstruct or halt the use of TT data in criminal investigations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is an injustice to the victims and those who are innocent who have placed their trust and confidence in our Police Force and our legal system.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These facts surely point to the original intent of TraceTogether, which is a technological/digitalisation measure that was put in place primarily for contact tracing in order to help our community contain the spread of the current pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The law enforcement benefits that may arise from this is only a useful byproduct and the CPC ensures that it will be used judiciously to serve societal needs for safety, security and pursuit of justice.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, this should not set the precedence and impact our safety and security by tying the hands of our Police as we move into the digital future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And let this be the only time where we limit access to information for our Police Force in the pursuit of justice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the past few months, the Bills, which have been fast-tracked all relate to COVID-19 measures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this is not simply an issue of privacy and data protection, it is also a public health concern.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Restoring the public’s trust in our national contact tracing infrastructure is important especially in these times.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We read in the papers news of second and third waves in other countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to be ready on all fronts to suppress any outbreaks as quickly as humanly possible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot now handicap ourselves by weakening the public’s trust in our contract tracing system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I should also say that I understand the public safety and security needs to access TraceTogether data for certain serious crimes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As a parent, if my daughters’ safety was at risk because of a kidnapping for example, I know I would want access to all data possible to keep them safe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The question is not whether the data should be used, but what safeguards should be in place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, the SPF may access TraceTogether data for a suspect involved in a murder investigation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the course of investigations, the TraceTogether data links the suspect to a separate petty theft committed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that police investigations are fluid, how does the SPF ensure that use of the TraceTogether data is strictly confined to the seven categories of serious crimes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what specific data points does the TraceTogether team use to measure the impact of the Government's announcement on TraceTogether app’s actual usage?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we look at daily active users or weekly active users, we might well notice no change in usage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we might find, for example, that more people are actually turning on the TraceTogether application only once a day and turning it off for the rest of the day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We may also find that mobile devices with TraceTogether apps are, on average, pinging with fewer devices than before, suggesting that the app or Bluetooth functionality may have been turned off.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even if we mandate that the app is flashed at point of entry to a location, a user can subsequently turn off the app.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I have said, I agree with the Government that TraceTogether data should be used for very serious crimes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we have to deal with the reality that some people may find ways around use of the TraceTogether app, compromising our public health efforts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The first truth: it is trite that comprehensive case investigation and contact tracing are crucial to prevent community spread of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition to vaccine, contact tracing and social distancing are our defences and instruments to fighting contagious diseases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are facing a global pandemic and an unprecedented economic crisis, the like of which our nation has never seen before.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a matter of life and death.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Conventional contact tracing and investigation is a complex and laborious process.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are also significant challenges like language barriers and distrust of unknown callers, coming in the wake of a year when online scams are increasing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Contact tracers are, in fact, in a race against time to prevent the next spread of infection.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the UK, by mid-July last year, the conventional contact tracing system was inundated and rendered less effective.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In London, only 47% of at-risk people were contacted.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The UK government had stated that in order for the tracing and curb to be effective, at least 80% of the infected people's contacts must be contacted and told to self-isolate within 48 to 72 hours.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's TraceTogether, which uses Bluetooth technology, is one of the least invasive of all the contact tracing tools out there.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, TraceTogether has been modelled by researchers in Germany who are working on an app which is compliant with the EU's General Data Protection Regulations (GDPR).

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: TraceTogether has assisted our agencies to quickly identify and curb local cluster transmissions in the community, as seen in the recent Police Para-Vet and Kallang industrial clusters.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is no doubt that contact tracing is vital in our fight against this pandemic and with more people using the app, the more effective our contact tracing will be.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The second unshakeable truth is that our law enforcement agencies have been effective in solving and deterring crimes, and as a result, we have built a reputation of being a safe and law-abiding country.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must give credit to the dedication and meticulous hard work of our Police officers over the years, aided by our robust legislation and criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our law enforcement agencies have been effective in thwarting threats to our public safety and security.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Just a week ago, we have been rocked by news of a foiled attempt to attack mosques in Singapore by a 16-year-old.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am confident that all Members of this House would agree on two things.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, that the offences specified are so egregious in nature and extremely time-sensitive that it is important to allow the Police to have all the tools at its disposal; and second, that there is no reason to doubt that the Police would use those tools judiciously and within the ambits of the law in order to fight such crimes quickly for the public interest.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, as part of our criminal law, the Police already has existing powers to compel production of any document or thing, including seizing computers or mobile devices.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The fact that the TraceTogether did not consider the application of the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) shows that the contact tracing tool was never designed for criminal investigations purposes in the first place.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Why not have a blanket exclusion of such data from criminal investigations?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I do not think we should go down this path because these are serious offences – the stakes are just too high.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   The success of TraceTogether is dependent on public trust and confidence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This debate has clarified how Police investigative powers, when using TraceTogether and SafeEntry data, are limited to only serious offences.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For someone who is under investigation for serious offences, the Police would have to firstly seize his or her mobile device, or TraceTogether token, before accessing the data, since the data is stored on his or her device.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is thus not a hidden attempt or something that is unknown to the individual.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, to further protect the rights of privacy of the individual, perhaps the Ministry can consider a dedicated channel within the PDPC to investigate any complaints of TraceTogether data access breaches made by any party.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another suggestion is in regards to the category of serious offences.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This includes those who by reason of their mental or physical incapacity, are unable to protect himself or herself.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have previously spoke about how we should, as a society, stand together to end violence and crimes committed against children and vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also believe that this will act as a deterrent to offenders who take advantage by hiding under the proverbial cloak of data privacy.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, this debate is not about fighting crimes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is about fighting the COVID-19 pandemic together as a nation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us not let this issue of data privacy distract us from what is at stake here.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We still have a long way to go in our fight against this pandemic, with the vaccination program being rolled out.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have to fight together as one and not allow any seeds of doubt to fester in our communities that will erode trust in our nation’s efforts to combat this pandemic and fight crimes at the same time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As the saying goes, "united we stand, divided we fall".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would not wedge the safety of my daughters or anyone's daughters – you can bet your bottom dollar on that.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The primary purpose of TraceTogether (TT), in the form of either a token or app, is to enhance contact tracing for COVID-19 cases and quickly locate the source of the infection.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, because it also records when and whom you have been in close contact with, that information might be useful to the Police when investigating certain cases, such as rape, kidnapping and murder, and allow them to apprehend the culprit in the shortest time possible.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Last month, the Straits Times reported a few sensational cases in Singapore in the past; these cases remain unresolved today.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some victims were raped before they were murdered.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As technology was not very advanced back then, even though the Police did a thorough investigation, they were still not able to apprehend the murderer.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As one can imagine, this has caused immense grief and anguish to the victims' family.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can imagine that to-date, they are still grieving and continue to hope that the Police can one day apprehend the murderer and bring closure to the case.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As technology becomes more advanced, we often see on Channel 8's Crime Watch how Police use certain technologies, such as CCTV footage and even leads provided on the media and social media platforms to solve crimes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, the investigation officers (IOs) in the Serious Crimes Division may also encounter tricky cases, for example, the culprits may have wiped clean their fingerprints in the crime scene and have not left any leads behind.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the crime scene, there were also no CCTV footages, so the Police were not able to locate the murderer.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: After the victim has died, family members may also turn to social media platforms and give out flyers to seek leads, but without any success.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When investigating such serious crimes, I think that the Police should do everything to fight against the clock, because as long as the murderer remains at large, it may cause others to panic and worry about their own safety.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In order to avoid another unsolved case, I agree that the authorities should reveal to the IOs information recorded by the TT.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This may bring a ray of hope in apprehending the culprits.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, the TT may also have recorded other people’s personal privacy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, I urge the authorities to be extra cautious and ensure that when using the information, other people’s personal data and privacy will not be leaked.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This public trust in the Government is especially important during a crisis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In line with what Prof David Chan explained in his book, "Combating a Crisis", public trust is directly affected by previous related events.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How agencies coordinate and work together as well as communicate with the public will also affect public trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
