text: We recall that last year, there were several incidents of data lapses or information leakage by public officers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This pertains to the number of COVID-19 cases and announcement of control measures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We also learnt about leaks involving personal data committed by public officers in violation of the Official Secrets Act in 2019.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And this was just months after the largest data breach in Singapore where personal data was stolen from SingHealth in 2018.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With these headline grabbing incidents, we can understand why the public may be concerned about their data collected through the TraceTogether platform.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On agencies working together, we should note that the TraceTogether initiative cuts across the portfolios of many Ministries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The gadget is developed as part of the Smart Nation initiative.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The data is channelled to MOH for contact tracing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And from the Government's response to a Member's Parliamentary Question last month, the public now knows that MHA, specifically the Police, has access to this data.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During my engagements with residents, I have encountered many instances where they asked me why it took so long for the Government to reveal this fact.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am glad that the Government has acknowledged that the issue should have been flagged earlier.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the West, technologies involving the mobile tracking of infectious diseases have been around for at least a decade.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, issues relating to privacy and civil liberty have contributed to such technologies’ low penetration rate in these countries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, it should not be surprising that Singaporeans, too, have concerns about individual’s data privacy even from the onset of the gadget roll-out.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe we can recall there were glowing news reports of hundreds who have enthusiastically queued at the various centres to collect their gadgets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Everyone then understood that the TraceTogether data would be automatically erased once it is older than 25 days and it would only be used by MOH.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: You can imagine the let-down when it was disclosed that the Police also have powers to access the data via the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is the data totally deleted and disappear after 25 days or is it still stored somewhere?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In order for Singapore to ride out this pandemic, we need all residents to be onboard the Government’s various measures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Apart from the ability to do effective contact tracing, we also need to vaccinate our population.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This, again, requires the people to trust the various types of information that the Government shares with the public, especially those related to vaccine safety.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Only with trust would people step forward and take the vaccination.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To do this, we must be clear when explaining or sharing information with the public.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If there is any misinformation, we must act at the earliest opportunity to set the record right.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, it is about the public’s belief that the Government is able to solve problems, be transparent, and says what it means and means what it says.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Deputy Speaker, it is up to the doer to undo the knot.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Indeed, considering how everything started, I am glad to hear the clarification made by the Minister just now and he had also assumed the responsibility.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He also acknowledged that because of the seriousness of the situation at that time, it was imperative to gather information to quickly identify, isolate and treat patients.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is expected that he and the departments involved had very limited time to think about any other ramifications.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although we are surprised and disappointed by this oversight, it is somewhat understandable, taking into account the unprecedented situation of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Now that the Minister has clarified it, I think the matter should be rested.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The reason is very simple: the Government obtains information through TraceTogether and the Criminal Procedure Code in order to protect its citizens.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government is unlike private companies, such as Google and Facebook which collect data to make a profit.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We do not seem to be as concerned about Google and Facebook collecting and monitoring our personal data and we often use these platforms.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, why are we so worried about the data the Government collects to protect us?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, what the Government collects, in comparison, is very limited and much less.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is more, we are a country governed by the rule of law, and there are rules governing data processing in all Government departments.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the course of implementation, institutional or personal lapses may occur occasionally, but once they are discovered, we acknowledge and rectify them.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is how we improve and strengthen the system.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Those who insist that it is too late for the Minister to take back his words, advocating personal privacy, and demand that the Government limit the TraceTogether data to COVID-19 tracing only, are missing the wood for the trees.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would ask, if not for our country bringing the pandemic here under control, and ensuring law and order, would we even be able to discuss privacy issues?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With hands and feet tied, how can the police solve cases and arrest suspects?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe that all Members here, including those in the opposition, will do their utmost to protect their families, protect their children, pursue all leads in order to identify the pervert, put him in jail and prevent him from endangering other innocent children.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is this value that has enabled us to fight the pandemic more effectively.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that the Minister will consider my views and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin and Mr Louis Ng asked about using contact tracing data for cases where the initial charge for a serious offence is subsequently reduced or amended to a less or non-serious offence, or if the serious offence reveals a separate non-serious offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is what we are trying to say in this Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There could be a situation where the suspect is investigated for both serious and non-serious offences committed at the same time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In criminal proceedings for such cases, which may be dealt with in a joint trial conference covering both the serious and non-serious offences, it would not be feasible to separate the data used for investigations of these offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But should the offences be dealt with separately in separate trials, then the prosecution will not be able to use the data in prosecution for the related non-serious offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked about Police’s use of TraceTogether data and Mr Leong Mun Wai also asked when Police first accessed the TT data.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Pritam Singh and Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin also asked about the usefulness of the contact tracing data for criminal investigations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is understandable that in any investigation, every piece of information is potentially useful and helpful.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In such a situation, contact tracing data could be critical information that we could use to identify any other persons involved in the planned attacks and uncover any terrorist ring as quickly as possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As you can see, when it comes to investigations, time is of the essence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If Police had intelligence and access to contact tracing data that could help stop attacks from taking place, I believe Members in this House would not say no.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked if we can give more than one example that Minister Vivian Balakrishnan had given in his opening speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Members can go through these scenarios and examples, and ask ourselves: would we really say that the information should not be used by the Police in such situations?

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I will let Members of the House read at your own time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling asked about the safeguards in Police’s access to the data.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: This is the same level of approving authority for bank data that we request from financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Second, within the Police, all requests for contact tracing data must be approved by the Criminal Investigation Department of the Singapore Police Force (SPF), which is the staff authority for all investigation-related matters within the SPF.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Any public sector officer, including Police, who uses or discloses the data for a non-serious offence would have committed an offence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Lastly, all extracted data will be encrypted and kept in strict confidence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Only authorised officers will have access to the encrypted data.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mechanisms will be put in place to ensure restricted access and to maintain logs on the officers who have accessed the data.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: And, of course, if the data is used in Court, it will be seen whether the offence does or does not fall within the seven specified categories.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Ms Jessica Tan cited a situation where an individual’s lost token was used to commit a serious crime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: As part of an investigation, Police will holistically assess the leads and evidence, including TT data, in cases where this may be obtained.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: If a person assisting in investigation claims that he had lost his TT token, this will also be looked into by the Police.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: My advice is that upon the discovery of the loss of the TT token, one should quickly get a replacement at any Community Club, so as not to compromise contact tracing efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: My Sylvia Lim asked about my statement in Parliament last month about accessing suspect’s and witness’ contact tracing data.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Under the CPC, Police are entitled to access data from anyone.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: What was meant was that, operationally, in order not to compromise investigations, Police are more likely to approach witnesses first for data, in order not to tip off suspects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: In this Bill, Police are empowered to access data from all persons for investigating the serious crimes that are set out in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked why the exact list of offences is not specified.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Describing the categories of scheduled offences, rather than the specified offences themselves, is an approach that we have employed in other Acts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: For example, the Extradition Act takes a similar approach.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The seven categories of offences relating to serious offences that will be obvious prima facie.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: It will not cover other sexual assault involving mentally challenged victims.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The Police cannot use contact tracing data that fall outside of the seven categories.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Should a Police officer make a request, the Smart Nation and Digital Government Office (SNDGO) and MOH would not be permitted to provide the data.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Various Members asked to expand the Police's use of contact tracing data to other offences that are not covered or not included in the seven categories, such as outrage of modesty or offences against vulnerable persons.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Indeed, the data would be useful and would assist the Police to solve these crimes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: However, we had to make a judgement call on the balance between the two imperatives of public health and public safety that Minister Vivian Balakrishnan talked about.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Outrage of modesty and offences against vulnerable persons are of grave concern to the Police and public but rank below the seven categories in seriousness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: This was a very tough balancing act for MHA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Nonetheless, I would like to assure Members that the Police will continue to investigate all offences even though they are not in the seven categories of serious offences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Ms Sylvia Lim and others spoke about Australia's model.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Singapore had to decide what model and what we value.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We score exceptionally well on safety and security because of the approach that we have taken and that we have decided on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I have a graphic here and I will distribute to Members via email at the end of today to illustrate this point – that we are here today, our security situation and safety is a result of the model and decision we have taken in terms of our law enforcement policy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I am heartened that many Members expressed their support and trust in the Police.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: This trust and support is very precious to us, which we will guard zealously.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I believe all of us are agreed – I am looking at the Leader of the Opposition – that we are facing a global life-and-death crisis which requires extraordinary measures.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I believe all of us are agreed that contact tracing – effective, rapid contact tracing – is essential as part of our response to dealing with COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I also venture that all of us in this Parliament are agreed that TraceTogether and SafeEntry, representing our digital contact tracing tools, have made a real difference to the effectiveness of our COVID-19 response.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Members will know that I am by training and instinct a doctor.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Perhaps one of the defects of being a doctor is that we focus very, very much on the individual – on the health and on the outcomes of the individual.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I want to say that so that you understand in context because what I want to do now is to share my personal timeline, through this journey.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We first stated that the Government would use TraceTogether data only for contact tracing simply because this was how and why we designed TraceTogether.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I can tell you all categorically, again, as a doctor and perhaps a techno-optimist, that the potential use of the data by the Police did not cross my mind or the mind of my engineers at all.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In fact, if you think about the features that we built in – encrypted, decentralised data, auto-purging after 25 days, encrypted identities, no GPS, no cellular connectivity – I think any fair-minded person with some appreciation of technology will know that what we had in mind was digital contact tracing.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We were not at all trying to create a surveillance tool.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I say this so that you understand my state of mind when I said what I said in June.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But what I said in June was wrong because in a sense, my own enthusiasm for the technology blindsided me and I did not read section 20 of the CPC.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Because the law of the land, is that the CPC – specifically section 20 – does authorise the Police to access many databases, including contact tracing data.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The next point is – when did I become aware that what I said was wrong?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Basically, what happened was at the end of October, I was asked: are you sure that the CPC does not apply, even for a murder case?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: When I received that query, I asked my staff – please go and double check.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I am not a lawyer but please go and double check what the legal provisions are.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Your next question should be: well, what did you do after that?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In fact, I have shared that in the last month, I had many sleepless nights and I engaged in several rounds of discussion with some of my senior Cabinet colleagues on whether we should carve out and, if we did, how should we carve out the contact tracing data from the application of the CPC.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: You will know that my own strongly held view at that point in time was that even if the CPC applied and even if we were going to make data available, we should exercise this with utmost restraint.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I was also aware that I had first made this assurance in this Chamber.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I think it was in June in this Chamber.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I told my staff regardless of the outcome of this internal review, we will come back here and we will clarify.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I believe it was in early December – about a month after I commenced this process of internal discussion.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I am sharing this with you so that you understand that there is nothing to hide.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In an ideal world, no mistake would have been made.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But I am now in a scenario where a mistake has been made and the real question then is how do we maintain trust when a mistake has been made?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I will come back to my instinct as a doctor.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Both the patient and the doctor hope that we will never make a mistake.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The most important ingredient in that trust relationship between a doctor and a patient is complete transparency – that if anything goes wrong, I will tell you and if anything needs to be fixed, I will do so, and I will go all out to remedy the problem if I can humanly do so.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: My answer to this question today – how do you maintain trust when a mistake has been made – is actually quite straightforward.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is no different from a complication in surgery.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Next, do the right thing rather than choosing the politically expedient option.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: You know I believe in transparency even if transparency is awkward and politically costly.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But it is better to be transparent than to double down on a mistake.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Better to be transparent, fix the error rather than to double down on your mistake.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: One further principle from my medical practice is beware of false dichotomies.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The false dichotomy I have heard today is that you have to choose between saving the life of a child and you have to choose between participation in digital contact tracing.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I believe by being completely open, transparent, answering every question, explaining and letting people see the purpose behind what we are doing and why we are doing it, I believe we can avoid this dichotomy.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I believe it is possible for us to continue to have perhaps the world's most successful contact tracing programme; and at the same time, deal with people's expectations that Singapore will remain safe and secure.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And that the Police are our guardians, our protectors.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And that the Police have acted at all times strictly within the ambit of the law in order to fulfill their higher mission to protect us.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In fact, there has been some debate how specific are our definitions.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But I believe that this Bill reflects the right balance between restricting the use of personal digital contact tracing data and, at the same time, enabling our Police to fulfil their duty to keep us safe – avoid false dichotomies.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I will just reiterate a few scenarios which you would have, in fact, in the annex in front of you.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If the next of kin of a murder victim asks the Police, "Please decrypt the TraceTogether data on his phone", would any of you refuse?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If the parents of a kidnapped child found the token and desperately asked the Police to unlock it, which one of you would refuse?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If a terrorist act is imminent, would you tie the hands of our Police and security forces?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I believe I know the answer to these questions, and, certainly, the majority of Singaporeans outside this House.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Singaporeans understand the need for Police to lawfully access information and I believe that public trust in our Police Force remains high, very high.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And as Foreign Minister who has had to travel to many parts of the world, this confidence and trust is a huge competitive advantage that Singapore has.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: On the question of public trust and public participation, let me, in a rather limited way, share some numbers with you.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: You know that for TraceTogether, we give people the option of writing in to say, "Please delete my data".

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Every one of that 350 who has requested us to delete is a source of regret for me.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I do not want to belabour this but my simple conclusion or inference is that Singaporeans know that I misspoke but they also trust the TraceTogether system is safe, it does what it is supposed to do, it protects public health, and they also trust the Police to always behave lawfully.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Members also had questions on the features and safeguards of TraceTogether and SafeEntry.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Mr Louis Ng, and I think Mr Pritam Singh as well, asked whether it has affected our adoption.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I have just given you some figures on people who have signed on in the last one month.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But I will also accept the point that Mr Louis Ng made, and I think Mr Gerald Giam made as well, that there may be individuals who are gaming the programme.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: You switch it on in order to do your SafeEntry and then you promptly switch it off.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I think Mr Louis Ng also asked whether we have more granular data into how people are using the tokens and using the TraceTogether app.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Based on broad proxies, and I say proxies, and I will explain why it is only a proxy, but based on broad proxies, we estimate about 58% of users use the app at least once a day.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This proportion has remained the same before and after the parliamentary clarification in January.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Mr Ng also asked if we could provide more granular usage statistics, such as whether the mobile devices with the applications were on average pinging fewer devices than before.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And, Mr Ng, I have to tell you, actually, the privacy-respecting nature of the system means we actually cannot collect that level of granular data to track active usage.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The data is stored locally on your own device.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The TraceTogether app only connects to the server periodically, only to download information.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Some Members would be familiar – occasionally, when you have checked into the same place as someone else who has turned out to be COVID-19-positive, that message may light up to warn you that there may be a potential overlap in time and space between you and the COVID-19-positive patient.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The point I am making is that, again, it reveals the privacy by design that we focused on in rolling out this programme.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I want to remind everyone that TraceTogether is meant to protect us and our loved ones.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The effectiveness of TraceTogether depends heavily on the rate of user participation.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: For those who switch off your Bluetooth or your app or engage in other forms of technical wizardry, I would just ask you why deprive yourself and your loved ones of the protection?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Again, as Foreign Minister, I have looked round the world and one of the reasons why we are better off is that we have not politicised our response to COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I am grateful to Mr Singh and the Workers' Party that, unlike in other countries where wearing a mask or not wearing a mask is a badge of political identity, we have avoided that kind of political dichotomy.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, for people who are angry or disappointed at my mistake, you are entitled to do that but do not deprive yourself and your loved ones of the protection from this system.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Ms Nadia Samdin asked a few suggestions regarding OpenTrace, and she asked if we would continue to make OpenTrace open-source such as by introducing open-source licences and regularly updating the GitHub repository.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Actually, my engineers will know that I have been leaning on them repeatedly to keep updating the GitHub repository.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But, again, those of you who are actual programmers will know it is a very big slog to tidy up your code and prepare it for public open-source perusal.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But we believe in open-sourcing OpenTrace, it has served us well, it has been helpful, it has allowed experts to look at both OpenTrace and TraceTogether, and for them to conclude that the app does and continues to do what it is supposed to do, and to do so in a privacy protecting manner.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Other governments have looked at our code base including Australia, Alberta, Poland.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We have had discussions at the technical level.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: They have modified it, used it, changed it; we are completely open about that.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: To be clear to Ms Nadia Samdin, there is already an open-source licence.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The OpenTrace repository is published under – sorry, to get technical here – a GNU General Public Licence Version 3.0.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Those of you in the know will know that this is an open-source licence.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The Standard General Public Licence 3.0 terms are also within the repository itself in a licence and markdown file, as is the standard practice, and maybe Ms Nadia Samdin can check on that after this.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But I will convey your suggestions to the GovTech team and discuss what our next steps are for open-sourcing.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Ms Nadia Samdin also asked if we would commit that TraceTogether data will always be stored on the user's device and shared with MOH only when the user uploads the data, and to delete the data at the request of the user.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: By design, TraceTogether data will be stored in the user's device before it is shared with the authorities.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Again, for those of you who have ever been in the circumstance where you need to share it, you know that your participation is needed.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The same applies for the suggestion on deleting the data upon request.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But in certain cases, for instance, where the data has already been uploaded because there was a positive COVID-19 case, then MOH will have to retain that data as long as that cluster is active and they need it in order to break the chains of transmission.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I am sure Members of this House will understand the need for that.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about the Police's use of SafeEntry data.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I believe the Member did ask just now.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I am not privy to the operational details but I do understand that SafeEntry data has been used for investigations into offences in a number of instances.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I must state for the record that my previous assurances were on TraceTogether in this House and not on SafeEntry.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is also worth reminding Members of the House that, actually, SafeEntry is a digital visitor log.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If it was not there, the Police would go to the security guard, say, of your condominium and say who has come in at what time, which car numbers were in here, look at your video surveillance.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: SafeEntry actually, in that sense, is not novel compared to TraceTogether.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But it is different in the sense that it is a centralised database.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Therefore, we decided we better take pre-emptive action to put the same cocoon of legislative protection around it.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Ms Nadia Samdin asked if an individual would be able to access their own personal contact tracing data including if one is being charged for a serious offence.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Members of the public can request for their own data for legitimate purposes as is the current practice today.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The lawyers looking at the text of the Bill will realise we have been very careful not to circumscribe the rights of the individual to his data.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I believe Ms Sylvia Lim asked if suspects and the Defence Counsel could access the personal contact tracing data for their Court cases and whether the time period of 25 days is sufficient to retain the data for such users.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: For serious offences, the individual can share his or her own data with anyone including the Police, the prosecution, the Defence Counsel and offer his or her data to the Court as evidence.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If the Prosecution is in possession of contact tracing data which strengthens the Defence's case or weakens the Prosecution's case, the Prosecution has to disclose such data to the Defence to comply with its common law disclosure obligations laid down by the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I believe this is known as the "Kadar disclosure obligations".

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The right of access under "any rule of law" here includes the Kadar disclosure obligations.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling asked if TraceTogether data could be used in missing persons cases.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: A next of kin – father, mother, husband, wife – a next of kin may request the data of a missing person to the extent permissible today.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This includes requesting for personal contact tracing data of the next of kin, if they have a right to do so.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Mr Gerald Giam also asked if personal contact tracing data uploaded to MOH servers would be covered by this Bill specifically by section 82.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The Bill restricts the Government's use of personal contact tracing data collected from digital contact tracing systems specified in the Sixth Schedule.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Mr Zhulkarnian Abdul Rahim suggested having a dedicated channel independent of the Police to investigate any complaints of TraceTogether data access breaches made by any party.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: These authorised persons would be appointed by Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean as the Minister overseeing this part of the Act.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, there is a clear separation of roles and duties.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: There were also other questions pertaining to data governance for personal contact tracing data.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It was Mr Yip who asked whether Police would still be able to request the data beyond the 25-day mark, and if the data will be stored for more than 25 days, should it be required by Police for investigations and proceedings into serious offences.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I think it was also Mr Giam who asked if Police will be able to access the data when the pandemic has been declared over.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In general, the Police will not be able to obtain data if the request comes in after the 25th day mark and this is because the data would have been auto deleted, either deleted on your personal token or app or deleted from the main server.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Nowadays, I am very careful with all my caveats.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: There are some exceptional scenarios where the data may be stored for more than 25 days.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: One, when the data relates to a COVID-19 patient or an individual who is closely associated with the patient, and the data is used for active contact tracing purposes.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And I think that, people will accept this is a legitimate use of data beyond the 25th day.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Two, when the data has been used for investigations or criminal proceedings in respect of serious offences; the data may be retained until the investigation or criminal proceedings are over, including Court proceedings, I must add, and will be deleted when the data is no longer needed.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The same applies to when the pandemic is being declared over.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And then we can happily stand down our digital contact tracing programmes.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: As I mentioned in my opening speech, subsection 82(8) provides for the Minister to specify a date after which digital contact tracing system is no longer required to prevent or to control the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The data administrator must then delete any personal contact tracing data which is no longer required.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Police will not be able to use any personal contact tracing data unless the data had previously been retained and used for investigations of criminal proceedings in respect of serious offences.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: My team will work out the details on how often and the contents of these reports, but it should broadly encompass the types of data, how the data was used, as well as the number of occasions that the data has been used for purposes other than contact tracing from the day that this Act comes into force.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin and Mr Gerald Giam asked if it was possible for us to specify the conditions for the life cycle of the TraceTogether programme, such as the conditions to decide when it should be deactivated.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Actually, this is a much wider question – what determines the changing points in the pandemic and what determines the end of the pandemic?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Our approach has to be guided by science and public health.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We will monitor the overall situation closely, consider all relevant factors before adjusting our measures, as we have indeed in the last one year with our three phases of re-opening since the circuit breaker.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In other words, there is no rule book.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: There is no standard play book that we can rely on.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We will have to respond to the situation as it evolves.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And this approach has served us well, and we should continue to abide by this considered approach in determining the end of the pandemic.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Even now, we know that the pandemic has been very unpredictable.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Many places that previously contained their initial infections, are now dealing with second, third, fourth waves.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: New variants have emerged, some more transmissible, some even more lethal.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Whether and when we can revert to normal will really depend on the global situation, not just the situation within Singapore and this is the nature of infectious disease epidemics.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Lastly, Members expressed a wide variety of views on the types of offences which Police ought to use personal contact tracing data for investigations or criminal proceedings.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Some of you suggested expanding the list, some to include additional offences.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Mr Vikram Nair, I believe, said that he preferred not to have any carve-outs.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: He said that this would be tantamount to saying that the Police should not look at all available information in pursuit of their investigations.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Mr Sharael Taha, Ms Tin Pei Ling, Mr Alex Yam and Mr Christopher de Souza expressed concerns that the passage of this Bill may set a precedent for how the Government may use data collected by digital solutions in the future, and hamper the Government’s ability to function effectively.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is intended to deal with the specific issue of the Government’s use of personal data collected via digital contact tracing systems in the midst of an emergency.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We have taken this exceptional step because we need to focus on encouraging public participation and maintaining confidence in our public health measures.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is not in the public interest to deny the Police access to the data necessary to ensure public safety and the proper conduct of justice.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Privacy and data governance, especially, in the face of accelerating technological revolution, these are broad and complex issues, which I think Mr Singh also recognises, that need careful contemplation, consultation and open debate.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This should not be settled on a Certificate of Urgency in one day.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: There will be proper occasions in the future to do this.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This current state of affairs did not happen by chance.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is due to our concerted efforts on multiple fronts – our excellent healthcare system, our heroic frontline officers, our extensive testing capacity, our effective contact tracing regime that has enabled us to quickly identify, isolate close contacts, truncate transmission.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Most of all, it is because of our social capital, the sacrosanct trust of our citizens and the collective responsibility that we have for one another.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am just reviewing the articles in our newspapers of record, The Straits Times, from end October right through early November.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A number of representations made by various Ministers nothing suggested that the Government was going to make the revelation that the Minister shared in early January clear that section 20 of the CPC would apply.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That actually came end October, a good two months later.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can I ask the Minister what was the Cabinet deliberating, if that was an issue with regard to the Cabinet?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Or what caused the delay in coming to a landing on the time and by when the Government will make things clear to Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The question actually that I asked and I think a few other Members asked was whether the Government or the Smart Nation Office or GovTech is able to track when people switched off their TraceTogether application.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because that really is the key because if for some reason people are not confident, then we have got a problem on our hands.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, how is it that the Government is able to track when people switch on their phones at least once a day, but for some reason is not able to find out when people turn off their phones?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The third point I think is not specific to Minister's speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is the Parliamentary system of Government we have here.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I know there are individual Singaporeans outside of this House who are concerned about the privacy issues and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I would just like to advise everyone, well, not everyone but those who are not comfortable with the Government's replies – all of us in the WP, as I know, have downloaded TraceTogether.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I would like to share with Singaporeans to please download the app and use the token, because it is the safety of the entire community that is at stake, insofar, as COVID-19 is concerned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Whatever concerns that are there that you wish to raise, I am sure your parliamentarians will bring them up in Parliament and certainly the Opposition in Parliament will do so.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: At the end of October, when I was asked, basically, what did I spend November doing?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: As I said, double checking the legislation and then having, among sleepless nights and conversations, asking: "Do we carve it out?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: What should we do?" So, that occupied us in November.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Mr Christopher de Souza filed in December and I thought it was right that we should answer it in Parliament.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If I could replay, if I could rewind time, I would not even have made this mistake in June.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And I would also say if I could replay, I would also have looked for an earlier occasion to explain all this.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But the key point which I am trying to make, is that there was never any doubt in my mind that we would clarify, that we would explain and we would be held accountable and that I would take responsibility.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And for myself having been being in this Chamber now for almost 20 years, the older Members will know, I have always operated that way.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Mistakes, warts, misunderstandings, misspeak – I have never shied away from clarifying it.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I think it was last month when you said you accept in good faith my explanation.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, never any attempt, to shy away from transparency and from reflecting the mistake.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: On the second question about why I said 58% switch it on at least once a day.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Again, if you look at your app, and if you see somewhere about the upper third, it will probably say you are okay.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: What it does in order to tell you whether you are okay or not, is that it has to query a central server as to whether the SafeEntry check-ins that you have done, have overlapped in time and space with someone else.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If you have, then some of you may receive a slightly more worrying message to say that this has happened.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If you have symptoms, please see a doctor and please get tested.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Now, of course, if we have identified you as a close contact on the basis of Bluetooth proximity data from TraceTogether, you do not need to wait for that message, we will call you, and test you and isolate you, if necessary.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But anyway, to come back to that question of, "How come you know I am on but I do not know when you are off".

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, I know you are on because you have actually queried the database to check whether your journeys overlapped with someone else who may have been positive.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But I do not know when you switch it off or when you, as Mr Gerald Giam has mentioned, put it in a Faraday Cage.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I do not know that, precisely because of the privacy respecting design of the system.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This also relates, although you have not asked it, to the question about how useful is TraceTogether data for Police investigations.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And again, I would reiterate my explanation that, by its very design, you know I was not designing a surveillance system.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, you can make a reasonable argument that therefore most times, it is not going to be very useful.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And for those of you who have served in the Police Force – Ms Sylvia Lim has, I believe, been a Police officer, Mr Murali has been a Police officer and Deputy Prime Minister Heng has been a Police officer – you will know that when you are investigating any leads, indirect, circumstantial or otherwise, may be relevant.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Please allow me some time to do that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Do you mean I am not allowed to —

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: You can clarify but please keep it succinct.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Since PSP is not going to support the Bill, I think it is our responsibility to explain to this House and to Singaporeans, our position further.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Sorry, this is seriously for clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, in that case, maybe I would like to ask the Minister that in deciding the trade-off, very often, he brought up the example of one victim of the seven serious crimes; maybe a victim of one of the seven serious crimes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Of course, I accept the explanation that he has done with regard to he does not think there is an effect on that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I would like him to clarify, what does he think about that approach to making the trade-off, which is the approach that PSP has taken.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, I would still appeal to your good sense and your sense of responsibility to the nation to do the right thing.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: That is why I stand here completely confident that we are doing the right thing.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is not the convenient thing for me personally, politically, but it is the right thing.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I hope PSP can do likewise, but that is your decision.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Leong, I think you have made your point already.
